Unit 11: Human Circulatory System

Short Questions

SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS EXERCISE

Q1. What is the main difference
between the walls of an artery and a vein?
Arterial walls
• The walls of
arteries are made
up of three layers.
• Outer layer i.e.,
tunica externa or
adventitia is made
of connective and
elastic tissue.
• Middle layer i.e.,
tunica media is
made of thick
muscular tissue
and elastic fibres.
• Inner layer i.e.,
tunica intima is
made of thin layer
of endothelial
cells.

Venous wall
• The wall of veins
has same three
layers as are
present in arteries.
• The outer layer
i.e., tunica
externa
(adventitia) is
made of
connective and
elastic tissue.
• The middle layer
i.e., tunica media
is relatively thin
and only slightly
muscular, with
few elastic fibres.
• The inner layer
i.e., tunica intima
is made of thin
layer of
endothelial cells.

Q2. Enlist the four valves present in
heart and also state their locations.
Ans. AV-Valves: At the entrance points of
ventricles (in atrioventricular septum), there
are two atrioventricular valves i.e., a
tricuspid valve and a bicuspid valve.
• Tricuspid valve (made of three cusps) is
present between right atrium and right
ventricle.
• Bicuspid (mitral) valve (made up of two
cusps) is present between left atrium and
left ventricle.
• Semilunar Valves: At the exit points of
ventricles, there are two semilunar valves
(with shapes like a half-moon).
There are two semilunar valves;
• Pulmonary valve is located at the base of
pulmonary artery between right ventricle
and pulmonary trunk.
• Aortic valve is located at the base aorta
between left ventricle and aorta.

Q3. State the phases of heartbeat.

Ans. There are three phase of heart beat.
1. Diastole: When atria are relaxed and being
filled with blood, the ventricles are also

[REPORT ANY MISTAKE AT: FREEILM786@GMAIL.COM] [WEBSITE: WWW.FREEILM.COM]

--- Page 2 ---
relaxed. This relaxed period of heart
chambers is called diastole.
2. Atrial systole: As blood accumulates in
atria, their blood pressure rises, due to
which both of them contract. This is called
atrial systole. It passes the blood through
tricuspid and bicuspid valves into the two
relaxed ventricles.
3. Ventricular systole: When ventricles are
filled with blood, both of them contract.
This is called ventricular systole and it
pumps the blood to pulmonary arteries and
aorta.
Duration: In one complete heartbeat,
diastole lasts about 0.4 sec, atrial systole
takes about 0.1 sec, and the ventricular
systole lasts about 0.3 sec.
Q4. List the principles and use of
Electrocardiogram.
Ans. Principle: When cardiac impulse
passes over the surface of heart a minute
electrical current is generated. This current
spreads into the tissues surrounding heart.
This minute electrical current also travels to
the surface of body.
• In ECG, the electrical potentials generated
by this current are measured and recorded.
For this purpose, electrodes are placed on
skin on the opposite sides of heart. The
electrodes are attached to a machine called
electrocardiograph that records electrical
potentials generated by this current.
Uses: ECG helps to diagnose the
abnormalities and abnormal rhythms in
conduction system of heart.
Q5. Define angiography and angioplasty.

Ans. Angiography
Coronary angiography is an X-ray
examination of blood vessels or chambers of
heart. In order to create the X-ray pictures, a
physician guides a small tube-like device
called catheter through the large arteries of
body fluid (contrast medium) is injected and
pictures (angiograms) are obtained.
Angioplasty
Angioplasty is a procedure that opens a
blocked or narrowed artery. During an
angioplasty, a small wire called a catheter,
under X-ray guidance is passed through the
narrowed coronary artery the balloon is
advanced through wire and inflated to dilate
the narrowed section of block artery.
Q6. What is meant by Purkinje fibres?

Ans. These are the network of fibres
formed by the division of AV-bundles in the
walls of ventricles. Stimulation of these
fibres causes the ventricles to contract almost
simultaneously.
Q7. What do you mean by
vasoconstriction and vasodilation?
Ans. Vasoconstriction: It is the decrease
in diameter of a blood vessel due to
contraction of smooth circular muscles, in
the walls of arterioles, under the effect of
nervous or endocrine stimulation. It
reduces blood flow in arterioles.
Vasodilation: It is the increase of diameter
of a blood vessel due to relaxation of smooth
circular muscles in arterioles. It increases
blood flow in arterioles.
Q8. What is the rate of blood flow in
different types of blood vessels?
Ans. Rate of Blood Flow
The velocity of blood flow is different in
different vessels. It is highest in aorta (450-
500 mm/sec) and tends to fall along the
network of arteries, arterioles and becomes
lowest in capillaries (01 mm/sec). It rises
again in venules, veins and vena cavae (250-
300 mm/sec). These changes in the velocity
of blood result from changes in the total
cross section of the vessel system.

--- Page 3 ---
[WANT TO GET ALL SUBJECT NOTES: WWW.FREEILM.COM]                                                               [WEBSITE: WWW.FREEILM.COM]

Q9. State the role of baroreceptors and
volume receptors in regulating the low
blood pressure.
Ans. Regulation of Blood pressure
Role of baroreceptors: Pressure receptors,
known as baroreceptors are present in
carotid arteries (arteries that supply blood to
the head region and brain) and aortic arch
(portion of aorta that bends between the
ascending and descending aorta).
When blood pressure falls, baroreceptors
activate sensory neurons that send
information to brain. The control centre in
brain reacts by increasing the rate and force
of contraction of heart and by causing
vasoconstriction in arterioles. Both these
changes restore blood pressure to normal.
Role of volume receptors: Certain
hormones regulate the volume of blood by
effecting the reabsorption of water and salt in
kidneys. When there is a decrease in blood
volume and blood pressure, special receptors
present in brain create thirst. They also
stimulate posterior pituitary gland to secrete
antidiuretic hormone (ADH).
Q10. Differentiate between thrombus and embolus.
Thrombus
Thrombus is a solid mass or plug of blood
constituents (clot) platelets, fibrin fibres in
a blood vessel. This mass may block
(wholly or only in part) the vessel.
Causes: Thrombus formation may be due
to; (i) irritation or infection of lining of
blood vessels, (ii) reduced rate of blood
flow, due to long periods of inactivity, or
(iii) pneumonia, tuberculosis, emphysema
etc.
Embolus
The dislodged thrombus which has entered
the blood circulation is called embolus.
Embolus may be carried to some other
locations in the circulatory system which
may get stuck in smaller blood vessels and
cease blood supply leading to death of the
affected tissues.

SLO BASED SHORT QUESTION ANSWERS
Structure and Functioning of Heart
Q11. Name the transport systems of
humans describe the composition of blood
circulatory system of humans.
Ans. Humans have two systems for the
transport of different materials in different
parts of body i.e., blood circulatory system
and lymphatic system.
• The closed blood circulatory system of
humans consists of blood, heart, and blood
vessels (arteries, capillaries and veins).
★Q12. Why heart is felt on the left side of
chest? Describe its relation with lungs.
Ans. The heart is usually felt to be on the
left side because the left side of heart is
stronger and larger, since it pumps blood to
all body parts.
Relation with lungs: Because the heart is
between the lungs, the left lung is smaller
than the right lung and has a cardiac notch
in its border to accommodate the heart
Q13. Describe the position and location
of heart.
Ans. It is situated in the middle of chest
cavity (between the lungs). Its back surface
is near vertebral column while its front
surface is behind sternum and rib cartilages.
Q14. What is pericardium? Describe its
layers with their roles.
Ans. Heart is enclosed in a sac called
pericardium. Pericardium separates heart
from surrounding organs. It is composed of
the two layers, pericardial cavity and
pericardial fluid.

[REPORT ANY MISTAKE AT: FREEILM786@GMAIL.COM]                                                               [WEBSITE: WWW.FREEILM.COM]

--- Page 4 ---
1. Outer layer of pericardium is called
fibrous pericardium. It is made of strong
connective tissue.
• It protects heart against external pressure
and shocks.
• It also prevents excessive dilation of heart.
2. Inner layer of pericardium is called
serous pericardium. It is a sac, made of
two layers i.e.,
a) Outer parietal pericardium - present
beneath fibrous pericardium.
b) Inner visceral pericardium (also called
epicardium) - closely attached to the
underlying heart.
Pericardial cavity: The space between
parietal and visceral pericardium is called
pericardial cavity.
• It contains up to 50 mL pericardial fluid.
It lubricates heart and protects it from
infections.
Q15. Describe the structure of heart
wall.
Ans. The heart wall is composed of three
layers.
Outer layer: The wall of heart is composed
of three layers. The inner layer of
pericardium i.e., epicardium makes the outer
lining of heart wall.
Middle layer: Beneath epicardium, there is
the thickest layer of heart wall i.e.,
myocardium. Myocardium is made of
cardiac muscles.
Inner layer: Endocardium is present beneath
myocardium. It is a single layer of epithelial
cells and make the inner linings of heart
chambers.

Q16. How many chambers are present in
heart? State chambers and septa of heart.
Ans. Chambers of heart
There are four chambers of heart i.e., two
upper thin-walled atria and two lower thick-
walled ventricles. Atria receive blood from
body and pass it to ventricles, which
distribute blood to body.
Septa of heart
• Atrioventricular septum: Atria and
ventricles are separated by
atrioventricular septum.
• Interatrial septum: The left and right
atria are separated from each other by an
interatrial septum.
• Interventricular septum: The left and
right ventricles are separated from each
other by an interventricular septum. It
is much thicker than the interatrial
septum.
Q17. Human heart functions as a double
pump. Justify?
Ans. Human heart functions as a double
pump because its right side (Right atrium
and Right ventricle) carries deoxygenated
blood, and its left side (left atrium and left
ventricle) carries oxygenated blood. It carries
out pulmonary circulation (supply of blood
to lungs) and systemic circulation (supply of
blood to all organs of body except lungs).
Complete separation of deoxygenated (right
side) and oxygenated (left side) blood is
maintained in heart.
Q18. Trace the circulation of blood
between heart, lungs and body.
Ans. Circulation of deoxygenated blood
The right atrium receives deoxygenated
blood from body via two veins i.e., superior
vena cava and inferior vena cava. Right
atrium passes this blood to right ventricle via
tricuspid valve. When right ventricle
contracts, deoxygenated blood is passed to

--- Page 5 ---
pulmonary trunk via semilunar pulmonary
valve. The pulmonary trunk divides into left
and right pulmonary arteries which carry this
blood to lungs.
Circulation of oxygenated blood
The oxygenated blood from lungs is brought
to left atrium by four pulmonary veins. Left
atrium passes this blood to left ventricle via
bicuspid (or mitral) valve. When left
ventricle contracts, oxygenated blood is
passed to aorta via semilunar aortic valve.
Aorta carries this blood to all parts of body
(except lungs).
Q19. Define heartbeat.
Ans. Definition: “The rhythmic contractions
and relaxations of the heart muscles, produce
sound is called heartbeat”.
Heart works in continuous cycles. Its
chambers relax and are passively filled with
blood from large veins. Then, its chambers
contract and propel the blood throughout
body.

Q20. Why left ventricle is thicker than
right one?
Ans. The wall of left ventricle is thicker
(about 3 times) than that of the right ventricle
because it has to push/pump the blood to all
over body, with greater force.
Q21. Differentiate between normal and
abnormal heart sounds. How abnormal
sounds can be caused?
Ans. Normal heart sounds: There are two
normal heart sounds heard by stethoscope.
Lubb sound: When both ventricles contract
simultaneously to pump the blood to
pulmonary arteries and aorta, the tricuspid
and bicuspid valves close and “lubb” sound
is made.
Dubb sound: When ventricular systole ends
and both ventricles relax simultaneously, the
pulmonary and aortic semilunar valves close
and “dubb” sound is made. Lubb-Dubb can
be heared with the help of a stethoscope.
Abnormal heart sounds: If the valves are
not closing fully, or if they open narrowly,
turbulence is created within the heart. This
turbulence can be heard; it is called murmur.
A murmur sounds like a hiss.

Q22. Compare the morphology and physiology of SA-node and AV-node.
SA-node
• The sinoatrial node consists of a small
cluster of cardiac muscle cells.
• It is embedded in the upper wall of right
atrium.
• Heartbeat starts when SA-node sends
electrical impulses to the walls of atria.
• It causes both atria to contract
simultaneously.

AV-node
• AV-node is made of small cluster of
cardiac muscle cells.
• It is located at the lower portion of
interatrial septum.
• It sends impulses to ventricles through
AV-bundle.

Q23. How nerve impulses are
propagated from AV-node to ventricles?
Ans. From AV node, the impulses reach an
atrioventricular bundle or bundle of His. It
is a network of fibres present in
interventricular septum. AV bundle divides
into left and right branches, which end at the
Purkinje fibres in the walls of the ventricles.
Stimulation of these fibres causes the
ventricles to contract almost simultaneously

--- Page 6 ---

Q24. What are consequences of blocked
or weak impulse in heart? How it can be
cured?
Ans. If there is some blockage in the flow
of the electrical impulses, or if the impulses
initiated by SA node are weak; it may delay
the rhythmicity of heartbeat or stop it, which
can lead to heart attack or cardiac failure, if
not cured.
Cure of weak impulses: In such patients of
weak SA node, artificial pacemaker is used.
It is a battery- operated device that is
surgically transplanted near the AV node. It
emits electrical signals that trigger normal
heartbeats.
Q25. Describe how heart rate is
controlled in various physical conditions?

Ans. The heart of an average adult beats
about 70 times per minute. It pumps the
entire blood volume (about 5 litres) every
minute. The normal speed of heartbeat is
made and maintained by pacemaker and AV
node. Brain also exerts some influence on
heart rate.
During fever: During fever and exercise, the
control centre in brain sends nerve signals to
both the pacemaker and the AV node, making
them to increase the heart rate. It is to cope
with the situation.
During rest: In contrast, when we are asleep
or at rest, the brain's control centre slows
down the activity of pacemaker and AV node.

wave form showing its component.
Q27. Compare PR segment with ST segment.
PR segment
• The flat line between the end of P-wave
and start of QRS complex is called PR
segment.
• It shows the completion of atrial
depolarization.
• It is usually 0.12 to 0.20 seconds.
• A prolonged PR indicates a first-degree
heart block.
ST segment
• It is a flat line between end of QRS
complex and start of T-wave.
• It shows the completion of
depolarization of ventricles.
• This segment ordinarily lasts about 0.08
second.
• It can be depressed in ischemia (decreased
flow of blood and oxygen to heart
muscles) and elevated in myocardial
infarction.

Q28. Brief about following components of ECG
a) P-wave b) T-wave
P-wave
• It shows beginning of atrial
depolarization, initiated by SA node. It
causes atrial contraction.
• Irregular or absent P waves may
indicate arrhythmia (lack of rhythmicity).
T-wave
• It represents the beginning of
repolarization of ventricles.
• T-wave abnormalities may indicate
electrolyte disturbance. The hyper-acute
T-wave shows the earliest findings of
acute myocardial infarction.

Q32. How capillaries are formed?
Describe their composition and role.
Ans. Formation: These vessels are formed
by the division of arterioles. Capillaries join
to form venules. Capillaries penetrate all
tissues and have approach to the cellular
level.
Composition: The walls of capillaries are
made of a single layer of endothelial cells.
The internal diameter of a capillary is about 8
micrometers.
Role: Capillaries are the sites where
materials are exchanged between blood and
body tissues by diffusion or active transport.
★Q33. What do you know about the length
of capillaries?
Ans. No cell of the body is more than 100
micrometres away from a capillary.
Capillaries are so narrow that RBCs must
pass through them in single line. It is
estimated that the total length of capillaries in
an adult human is over 80,600 kilometres,
enough to encircle the global twice!
Q34. Define interstitial fluid. Describe its
composition.
Ans. Definition: The pressure within
capillaries causes a continuous leakage of
fluid from the blood plasma into tissues. This
fluid, known as interstitial fluid.
Composition: Interstitial fluid consists of
water with dissolved nutrients, hormones,
gases, wastes and small proteins.
Large proteins, RBCs and platelets remain
within capillaries. But some WBCs can
squeeze out through the intercellular spaces
of capillary wall.
Q35. Describe the role of pre-capillary
sphincters in maintaining blood flow in
capillaries.
• Some capillaries are connected to arterioles
and venules through loops of other
capillaries. The entry of each loop is
guarded by a ring of muscles called a pre-
capillary sphincter These sphincters
regulate the amount of blood flowing
through capillaries.
• The amount of blood flowing in capillaries
is controlled by constricting or dilating the
capillaries. Nervous stimulation can
constrict capillaries and certain chemicals
such as histamine can dilate them.

Q36. Differentiate between pulmonary circulation from system circulation.
| Pulmonary Circulation | System Circulation |
| :--- | :--- |
| • Circulation of blood from heart to the lungs and from lungs back to the heart is called pulmonary circulation. | • Circulation of blood from heart to body (except lungs) and from body back to heart is called systemic circulation. |
| • Pulmonary circulation supplies deoxygenated blood to lungs and returns oxygenated blood to heart. | • The systemic circulation supplies oxygenated blood to all the cells, tissues, and organs of the body (except lungs) and returns deoxygenated blood to heart. |

[REPORT ANY MISTAKE AT: FREEILM786@GMAIL.COM]                                     [WEBSITE: WWW.FREEILM.COM]

--- Page 9 ---
Q37. Describe the blood supply of heart.
Ans. Arterial blood supply: The heart walls are supplied with blood through a small portion of the systemic circulation. Two coronary arteries i.e., the right and left coronary arteries, arise from the aorta, near its origin. These arteries divide into many smaller arteries, arterioles and then into capillaries.
Venous blood supply: After supplying oxygenated blood to heart muscles, the capillaries unite to form venules which make many coronary veins. The coronary veins join to form a coronary sinus, which opens in right atrium. Small coronary veins drain directly into right atrium.
Q38. Define hepatic-portal circulation. For what purpose it is build?
Ans. A portal system is a circulation in which veins end in capillaries. In hepatic portal system, a large hepatic portal vein collects blood from spleen and alimentary canal and takes it to the liver through hepatic portal vein. The blood from liver is taken to heart through hepatic veins. Hepatic portal system extends from thelower portion of oesophagus to the upper part of anal canal.
Purpose: The blood that comes from alimentary canal to liver contains substances that are absorbed from small intestine. These substances pass through liver before going to heart. Liver removes harmful substances from blood and absorbs nutrients for storage before sending this blood to heart.
Q39. Describe the renal circulation of blood.
Ans. Arterial circulation: The kidneys (renals) are supplied by left and right renal arteries. Right and left renal arteries carry oxygenated blood to the right and left kidneys. Inside the kidney, each renal artery divides repeatedly to make smaller arteries. The smaller arteries branch into several afferent arterioles, which supply blood to nephrons (units of kidney).
• Each afferent arteriole divides to make the capillaries of glomeruli.
Venous circulation: The capillaries of glomeruli unite to make efferent arteriole, which divides to make two sets of capillaries i.e., (i) peri-tubular capillaries (around nephron tubule in cortical portion of kidney), and (ii) vasa recta (around nephron tubule in the medulla of kidney). These capillaries unite to form venules that converge and make smaller veins. The smaller veins unit to form a renal vein.

Blood Pressure
Q41. Define blood pressure. Describe systolic and diastolic pressure. How it is measured?
Ans. Blood pressure is the measure of force exerted by blood against the inner walls of blood vessels arteries. This force keeps blood flowing from heart to the entire capillary network in body.
Systolic pressure: When ventricles contract (ventricular systole), heart forces blood into pulmonary arteries and aorta. As a result, the pressure in these arteries rises sharply. The

--- Page 10 ---
maximum pressure during ventricular systole
is called systolic pressure. Systolic pressure
in a normal young adult is 120 mm Hg.
Diastolic pressure: When ventricles relax
(diastole), the arterial pressure drops. The
lowest pressure that remains in arteries
before the next ventricular contraction is
called diastolic pressure. Diastolic pressure
in a normal young adult is 80 mm Hg.
• It is measured using sphygmomanometer
and stethoscope.
Q42. Describe the long-term regulation
of blood pressure. / Describe the hormonal
mechanism of blood pressure regulation.

Ans. The long-term regulation of blood
pressure is done through hormones. Certain
hormones regulate the volume of blood by
effecting the reabsorption of water and salt in
kidneys.
Role of ADH in low blood pressure
When there is a decrease in blood volume and
blood pressure, special receptors present in
brain create thirst. They also stimulate
posterior pituitary gland to secrete
antidiuretic hormone (ADH). ADH
stimulates kidneys to retain more water in
blood, excreting less in urine. It restores the
blood volume and ultimately blood pressure.
ADH also constricts arterioles, which raises
arterial blood pressure.

Q43. Compare and contrast the roles of ADH and ANH in maintaining blood pressure.
ADH
• ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormones) usually
works to raise/increase blood pressure
during low blood pressure.
• ADH stimulates kidneys to retain more
water in blood, excreting less in urine. It
restores the blood volume and ultimately
blood pressure. ADH also constricts
arterioles, which raises arterial blood
pressure.

ANH
• ANH (Arterial Natriuretic Hormones)
works to decrease blood pressure during
high blood pressure.
• The walls of right atrium contain endocrine
cells that secrete atrial natriuretic
hormone (ANH). When there is stretching
of the atrium by an increased blood volume,
the right atrium secretes ANH. It speeds up
the excretion of salts and water through
urine, which lowers the blood volume and
pressure.

Cardiovascular Disorders
Q44. Differentiate between atherosclerosis and arteriosclerosis.
Atherosclerosis
Atherosclerosis means deposition within
arteries. Various materials may accumulate
in arteries e.g., fatty materials, abnormal
amounts of smooth muscle cells,
cholesterol, fibrin and cellular debris of
various kinds.
Atherosclerosis can lead to heart attacks,
because it causes the narrowing of arteries

Arteriosclerosis
Arteriosclerosis means hardening of
arterial walls. It occurs when calcium is
deposited in arterial walls. The blood flow
through these arteries is restricted and
arteries cannot expand normally. This forces
the heart to work harder. Severe
atherosclerosis usually leads to
arteriosclerosis.

--- Page 11 ---
and increases the risk of the formation of
thrombus.

It is coexisting Atheroma and
arteriosclerosis Atheroma is deposition of
hard yellow plaque of lipoid material in the
inner most layer of arteries which may be
due to high level of cholesterol in the blood.
Arteriosclerosis is degenerative arterial
change associated with advancing age,
primarily a thickening of middle layer of
arteries.

Q45. Define thromboembolism and
thrombosis. How it is formed?
Ans. Thromboembolism: Formation of
thrombus in a blood vessel and then its
carriage to any other location is called
thromboembolism.
Thrombosis: Thrombosis is the formation of
thrombus. Thrombus is a solid mass or plug
of blood constituents (clot) in a blood vessel.
This mass may block (wholly or only in part)
the vessel.
Causes: Thrombus formation may be due to;
(i) irritation or infection of lining of blood
vessels, (ii) reduced rate of blood flow, due
to long periods of inactivity, (iii) pneumonia,
tuberculosis, emphysema etc.
Q46. What happens if thrombosis occurs
in coronary arteries and brain vessels?

Ans. Thrombosis blocks the blood flow to
organs. A thrombosis in coronary arteries
causes heart attack which can be life
threatening. Similarly, a thrombus in the
vessels of brain causes stroke (which causes
paralysis of the muscles). A thrombus may be
dislodged and carried to some other locations
in the circulatory system. Such a thrombus is
called embolus.
Q47. What is angina pectoris? What
does it indicate?
• The pain felt in the regions of chest,
shoulders, arms and jaws due to hypoxia
(low oxygen levels) to myocardium is
called angina pectoris.
• It usually occurs due to blockage of
coronary arteries is usually due to gradual
build-up of lipids (especially cholesterol)
in the inner wall of coronary artery.
• Angina indicates that oxygen demands are
greater than its delivery and a heart attack
may occur in future.
Q48. Define myocardial infarction. Is it
possible to recover from heart attack?

Ans. Death of heart muscles due to
insufficient supply of oxygen and nutrients;
leading to death of cardiomyocytes is known
as myocardial infarction also known as
heart attack.
Causes: The major cause of heart attack is
the blockage of coronary arteries.
Coronary arteries supply oxygen and
nutrients to cardiac muscles. If blood flow is
blocked in coronary arteries, it results in
insufficient supply of blood to one or more
parts of cardiac muscle.
Recovery from a heart attack is possible if
the damaged portion of heart is small enough
that the other blood vessels in heart can
enlarge their capacity and resupply the
damaged tissues.
Q49. Which procedure is used to
examine blood vessels and chambers of
heart? How it is performed?
Ans. Coronary angiography is the most
appropriate method to examine blood vessels

--- Page 12 ---
and heart chambers. In this method X-rays
are used to examine the blood vessels and
heart chambers. In order to create the X-ray
pictures, a physician guides a small tube-like
device called catheter through the large
arteries of body. When the tip of catheter
reaches the opening of coronary arteries, a
special fluid (called a contrast medium or
dye) is injected in catheter This fluid is
visible in X-ray machine. Pictures
(angiograms) of fluid in coronary artery are
obtained.
Q50. What is open-heart surgery? How
coronary bypass surgery is performed?

• The open heart surgery is done when
heart is still beating it includes bypass
surgery valvular replacement etc.
Coronary Bypass Surgery
• It is one of the most common and effective
procedures to compensate the blockage of
blood to cardiac muscles. In this surgery,
surgeon takes a healthy blood vessel from
leg, arm, chest or abdomen of the patient.
He attaches the ends of blood vessel above
and below the blocked coronary artery. So,
blood is bypassed around the damaged or
blocked area.
• Coronary bypass surgery doesn't cure the
underlying disease process i.e.,
atherosclerosis or coronary artery disease.
Lifestyle changes especially smoking
cessation are crucial to reduce the chance
of future blockages and heart attacks, even
after successful bypass surgery.
Q51. Describe the procedure of
performing angioplasty and stenting.

Ans. Angioplasty: Angioplasty is a
procedure that opens a blocked or narrowed
artery. During an angioplasty, a small wire
called a catheter, under X-ray guidance, is
passed through the narrowed coronary artery.

A small sausage- shaped balloon is then
advanced over the wire into the narrowed
section of artery. The balloon is then inflated
to dilate the narrowed section of the artery.
Once the artery is dilated, a small amount
of dye is injected to confirm the successful
dilatation.
Stenting: Stenting may also be done during
angioplasty. A stent is an expandable stainless
steel mesh tube, mounted on a balloon
catheter. When the stent/balloon is positioned
within the narrowed artery, the balloon is
inflated. The inflated balloon expands the
stent and the artery. The balloon is removed
and the stent remains in place. The stent
supports the artery walls and keep the artery
open and dilated.
Q52. Define hypertension. What are its
causes?
Ans. A chronic (long lasting) elevation
in blood pressure is called hypertension.
It occurs when blood pressure consistently
remains above 140/90 mm Hg.
Causes
• Any abnormality in nervous or hormonal
mechanisms of blood pressure regulation
may cause hypertension.
• Stress, obesity, high salt intake, smoking,
there may also be hereditary reasons of
hypertension.
Q53. Illustrate the damages caused by
hypertension. / What are the complications
of hypertension?
Ans. Whenever blood pressure is
chronically elevated, there is an increased
chance of the rupture of blood vessels.
Effect on brain: When this occurs in
brain, it is called brain haemorrhage. It
damages the delicate structure of brain.
Effect on cardiac muscles: Hypertension
also weakens cardiac muscles. If
hypertension is prolonged, heart is unable
to pump effectively and blood flow cannot

--- Page 13 ---
be maintained to meet needs of tissues. In
such conditions, blood may be retained in
heart and lungs. It is called congestive
heart failure.
Effect on kidneys: Hypertension can also
damage the nephrons of kidneys. It leads to
further retention of salts and water in blood
and therefore further hypertension.

Lymphatic system of human
Q54. Write the definition and
composition of lymphatic system of human.

Ans. In human, in addition to the blood
circulatory system, there is another system
responsible for the transport of materials. It
also returns the materials from tissues to
blood. This system is called lymphatic
system.
Composition: It consists of lymph vessels,
lymphoid masses, lymph nodes and lymph-
the fluid which flows in the system.
Q55. Define lacteals. Write their role.

Ans. The branches of lymph capillaries in
villi, are called lacteals. Fatty acids and
glycerol are absorbed into the epithelial cells
of villi where they form triglycerides. The
triglycerides are coated with proteins to form
chylomicrons, which enter the lacteals of
villi.
Q56. Write two important functions of
lymphatic system.
Ans. Functions of lymphatic system
• Lymphatic system returns the excess fluid
and dissolved proteins and other
substances to blood. In an average person,
about three litres more fluid leaves blood
capillaries daily. But it is absorbed by
lymphatic capillaries and returned to
bloodstream, before the blood enters heart.

• Lymphatic system also helps to defend
body against foreign invaders.
• Lymph nodes filter lymph. They have
lymphocytes and macrophages that destroy
bacteria and viruses present in lymph.
★Q57. Give the reason of swelling of
lymph nodes.
Ans. The painful swelling of lymph nodes
in certain diseases (e.g., mumps) is largely a
result of the accumulation of dead
lymphocytes and macrophages.
Q58. Define lymph nodes. Where the are
present in human body?
Ans. At certain spots, the lymph vessels
have masses of connective tissue where
lymphocytes are present. These are lymph
nodes. Several afferent lymph vessels enter a

INQUISITIVE QUESTIONS
Q1. Why is the pressure in the pulmonary circulation lower than in the
systemic circulation?
Ans. The pressure in the pulmonary circulation is significantly lower than is systemic
circulation due to differences in vascular resistance, vascular structure and functional
requirements. The pulmonary circulation is a low pressure, high flow system designed for
efficient gaseous exchange, while systemic circulation is a high pressure system needed to
supply all organs against resistance.
Q2. Why is it so important for the human heart to develop early and begin
functioning within the developing embryo?
Ans. The early development and functioning of the human heart in the embryonic life are
crucial for several reasons related to oxygen supply, nutrients delivery, removal of
metabolic waste and for the survival of embryo. Embryo grows too fast, so diffusion alone

[REPORT ANY MISTAKE AT: FREEILM786@GMAIL.COM]                                     [WEBSITE: WWW.FREEILM.COM]

--- Page 15 ---
becomes insufficient to meet the requirements of rapid growth. As the metabolic rate of
embryo is very high every. To form new organs, oxygen, nutrients supply and waste removal,
without heart seems to be very difficult.
Q3. Justify how vasoconstriction or vasodilation is reflective of emotions.

Ans. Vasoconstriction and vasodilation are physiological responses that reflects emotional
states due to relationship with autonomic nervous system and endocrine systems.
• For example, during fear stress & emergency situations sympathetic nervous system
activates leading to vasoconstriction in gastro intestinal tract (GIT) and skin while
vasodilation occurs improving blood flow to muscles and brain to prepare body for rapid
actions (e.g., running or fighting). These vascular charges not only prepare the body for
action or recovery, but also visibly manifest emotions (e.g., blushing, pallor) making them
a physiological mirror of our inner feelings.
Q4. Justify in what way the blood circulatory system is dependent on the
lymphatic system.
Ans. The blood circulatory system depends on the lymphatic system as about 3 litres more
fluid leaves blood capillaries daily then is reabsorbed in an average adult, lymphatic system
returns this excess fluid having dissolved proteins and other substances, back to blood
circulatory system to maintain its blood volume, moreover it also destroys the pathogens
which entered the tissues thus, helps defend the body against foreign invaders.
Q5. Interpret why the swelling of the lymph nodes is a cause of concern.

Ans. The swelling of lymph nodes also called lymph adenopathy can be caused by various
factors, like viral infections (mumps), bacterial infections (cervical lymph adenopathy) or
due to cancer. As the lymph nodes filter lymph bacteria or viruses present in lymph are
destroyed by macrophages and lymphocytes of lymph nodes which often result in swelling,
so that's why swelling of lymph nodes is a cause of concern it shall not be left unattended.
Q6. Trace the path of lymph until it is returned to the blood.
Ans. Lymph → lymph capillaries → lymphatic vessels → larger lymph ducts → main
lymph duct (right lymphatic duct and thoracic duct) → subclavian veins (right and left).

Unit 12: Human Skeletal and Muscular Systems

Long Questions

DESCRIPTIVE QUESTIONS

BONES AND CARTILAGE

Q1. Explain the structure of bone. / Describe the structural and chemical
composition of bone.
Ans. Skeleton
Bones, cartilage and other connective tissues make an internal framework called skeleton
that provides structural support, protects vital organs, and produces movement and
locomotion.
Structure of Bone
Bones are made of connective tissue reinforced with calcium and specialized bone cells.
Following are the major components of a bone;
1. The bone's surface is covered by a tough membrane called periosteum.
★The broad ends of a bone are called epiphysis while the middle part along the length of
bone is called diaphysis or shaft.
2. Compact Bone / Haversian System
The thick layer under periosteum is made of hard material and is called compact bone. It
makes up the majority of the bone tissue. The basic structural units of compact bone are
called Haversian systems. A Haversian system is made of three parts;
(i) Lamellae: These are concentric layers of mineralized extracellular matrix that contains
collagen fibres and small, needle-shaped crystals of calcium phosphate. The crystals are
brittle but rigid, giving bone great strength. Collagen, is flexible but weak. As a result, bone
is both strong and flexible.
(ii) Lacunae and Osteocytes: The lamellae are separated by small spaces called lacunae.
Osteocytes, which are mature bone cells, are located in the lacunae. Osteocytes are
connected to each other and to the Haversian canal by small channels called canaliculi.
(iii) Haversian canal: The concentric layers of lamellae surround a central canal called the
Haversian canal. It contains blood vessels, nerves, and lymphatic vessels.
Small Channels: There are small channels that run perpendicular to the Haversian canals
and connect them with each other and with the periosteum.
3. Spongy Bone: Beneath the compact bone there is spongy bone. It has a latticework
structure consisting of bony spikes that make it light and strong.
★ Note: All questions and paragraphs marked with a star ★ are explanations of the Box
Information provided in the textbook.

4. Bone Marrow
Many bones also contain a soft tissue called bone marrow, which can be either red or yellow.
(i) Red bone marrow is found in spongy bone, the ends of long bones, ribs, vertebrae, the
sternum, and the pelvis. It produces blood cells.
(ii) Yellow bone marrow fills the shafts of long bones. It consists mostly of fat cells and
serves as an energy reserve. It can also be converted to red bone marrow and produce
blood cells when severe blood loss occurs.
★Living tissues: Despite their number and size bones make up less than 20% of the body's
mass. Bones are not dry, rigid structures, as they appear. They are moist, living tissues.
5. Types of Bone Cells
There are three types of cells i.e., osteoblasts, osteocytes, and osteoclasts involved in the
development, growth and remodelling of bones.
• Osteoblasts are bone forming cells that synthesize and secrete unmineralized ground
substance. Once the osteoblasts are surrounded by matrix, they become the osteocytes.
• Osteocytes are mature bone cells which maintain healthy bone tissue by secreting
enzymes and bone mineral content. They also regulate the calcium release from bone
tissue to blood.
• Osteoclasts develop from macrophages and are involved in bone resorption, i.e., they
break down bone and release calcium and phosphate in blood. The work of osteoclasts
is important to the growth and repair of bone.
Q2. Illustrate the process of bone formation or osteogenesis. / OR
Define osteogenesis. Describe the primary pathways of osteogenesis. / Explain
the process of bone development.
Ans. Bone Development
Definition: "The process of bone formation is called osteogenesis."
It begins during embryonic development and continues throughout life, playing a vital role
in growth, maintenance, and repair of bones.

[REPORT ANY MISTAKE AT: FREEILM786@GMAIL.COM] [WEBSITE: WWW.FREEILM.COM]

Types of Bone Cells
There are three types of cells i.e., osteoblasts, osteocytes, and osteoclasts involved in the
development, growth and remodelling of bones.
• Osteoblasts are bone forming cells that synthesize and secrete unmineralized ground
substance. Once the osteoblasts are surrounded by matrix, they become the osteocytes.
• Osteocytes are mature bone cells which maintain healthy bone tissue by secreting
enzymes and bone mineral content. They also regulate the calcium release from bone
tissue to blood.
• Osteoclasts develop from macrophages and are involved in bone resorption, i.e., they
break down bone and release calcium and phosphate in blood. The work of osteoclasts
is important to the growth and repair of bone.
★ Even after bones have fully formed osteogenesis continues in the form of bone
remodelling. This ongoing process involves the breakdown of old bone by osteoclasts and
the formation of new bone by osteoblasts.

[Image of bone cells]
Osteogenic cell          Osteoblasts              Osteocyte              Osteoclast
(stem cell)           (form bone matrix)      (mature bone cell)       (resorbs bone)

                                Fig: Types of bone cells

Pathways: There are two Primary pathways of osteogenesis.
1. Endochondral Ossification/Transition of Cartilage into bone: The formation of long
bones e.g., femur and humerus, involves the transition of cartilage into bone. In this
process, the center of cartilage begins to harden (calcify), and the chondrocytes (cartilage
cells) in this area die, leaving behind cavities.
Ossification: The step by which cartilage is replaced by bone by the deposition of minerals
is called ossification. Blood vessels penetrate these cavities and introduce osteoblasts and
osteoclasts. Osteoblasts (bone-forming cells) start building bone tissue, replacing the
cartilage with new bone. Osteoclasts (bone-resorbing cells) break down the calcified
cartilage, making room for more bone tissue to form. As the bone matures, some osteoblasts
become trapped within the bone tissue and transform into osteocytes (mature bone cells),
which help maintain the bone structure. This process continues until all cartilage is changed
to a bone except some cartilage that remains only at the articular (joint) surfaces of the
bones.

2. Intramembranous ossification: The short bones develop directly into hard bone without
forming cartilage first e.g., some bones of the skull.
• In these cases, the osteocytes are initially scattered randomly throughout the embryonic

Q3. Describe the structure of cartilage and its types.
Ans. Definition: Cartilage is a type of connective tissue, which is made up of
perichondrium, cartilage matrix and chondrocytes.
Structure of Cartilage
1. Perichondrium: A layer of connective tissue called perichondrium surrounds the
cartilage. It contains blood vessels, lymphatic vessels, and nerves that supply the cartilage
tissue.
2. Cartilage matrix: Inside perichondrium is the cartilage matrix which is composed of
collagen, elastin, proteoglycans, and other fibres. It gives the tissue its strength, flexibility,
and resistance to compression. Unlike other connective tissues, there are no blood vessels
inside cartilage matrix. The cells of cartilage are supplied by diffusion. Because of this, it
heals very slowly.
3. Chondrocytes: The cartilage cells, called chondrocytes, are present within small spaces
called lacunae, which are embedded in cartilage matrix. Chondrocytes are responsible for
synthesizing and maintaining the matrix of cartilage.
Most of the cartilage of foetus is replaced by bone. However, some cartilage remains
throughout life and provides flexibility. For example, at the areas between bones, at the end
of nose, in the outer ear, and along the inside of the trachea.

4. Types of Cartilage
• Cartilage can be classified into three types.
• Hyaline cartilage is the most common type and is found in the nose, trachea, and the
articulating surfaces of bones in joints.
• Fibrocartilage is found in areas of the body that experience high stress and tension,
such as the intervertebral discs and the pubic symphysis.
• Elastic cartilage is found in the external ear and epiglottis.

The axial skeleton forms the axis of the body. It is composed of 80 bones. Its bones

Q5. Describe the arrangement of bones of human Appendicular skeleton.

Q6. Define joints. Write a detailed classification of joints.
Ans. Joint: A joint is a place where two bones or bone and cartilage come together.
Types: Three major kinds of joints are found in human body on the basis of structure i.e.,
fibrous (immoveable) joints, cartilaginous (slightly moveable) joints and synovial (freely
moveable) joints.
1. Fibrous Joints: In fibrous joints, the bones are directly connected to each other by
fibrous connective tissue consisting mainly of collagen. These joints permit no movement of
bones.
Examples of fibrous joints include:
• Sutures that occur only between the immovable bones of the skull.
• Joints between the tibia and fibula bones in the lower leg.
• Joints between teeth and their sockets in the jawbone.
2. Cartilaginous Joints: In these joints, the bones are connected by a layer of cartilage.
Cartilaginous joints allow little movement of the bones.
Types: There are two main types of cartilaginous joints:
i. Primary cartilaginous joints (synchondrosis): In some cartilaginous joints, the bones
are connected by hyaline cartilage. For example, the joint between the first rib and
sternum (sternocostal joint).
ii. Secondary cartilaginous joints (symphysis): In some cartilaginous joints, the bones are
connected by fibrocartilage. For example, pubic symphysis in the pelvic girdle and
intervertebral discs.

3. Synovial joints
A type of joint which is characterized by a fluid filled cavity surrounded by a fibrous
capsule. Synovial joints are the most common type of joint in the human body, and they
allow a wide range of movement.
Components of synovial joint
Synovial joint is composed of:
• Articular cartilage
• Fibrous capsule (joint capsule)
• Synovial fluid
• Ligaments
Articular Cartilage: A smooth,
tough, and elastic hyaline cartilage,
called articular cartilage, covers the
ends of the bones in the joint. It
provides a smooth and frictionless
surface for movement.

Fibrous Capsule: A fibrous capsule surrounds the synovial joint and helps to hold the
bones together. The fibrous capsule is composed of an outer layer of ligaments and an inner
lining of synovial membrane.
Synovial Fluid: Synovial membrane secretes synovial fluid, which lubricates the joint.
Ligaments: Strong bands of connective tissue that connect the bones in the joint are called
ligaments.

Q7. Define synovial joint. Classify synovial joints on the basis of range of motion. / Define synovial joint. Write its components and classification.
Ans. Definition: A type of joint which is characterized by a fluid filled cavity surrounded by a fibrous capsule.
Components of synovial
joint
Synovial joint is composed
of:
• Articular cartilage
• Fibrous capsule (joint
capsule)
• Synovial fluid
• Ligaments
Articular Cartilage: A
smooth, tough, and elastic
hyaline cartilage, called

movement.
Fibrous Capsule: A
fibrous capsule surrounds

The fibrous capsule is

of ligaments and an inner

membrane.
Synovial Fluid: Synovial
membrane secretes
synovial fluid, which
lubricates the joint.
Ligaments: Strong bands of connective tissue that connect the bones in the joint are called
ligaments.
Classification: There are six main types of synovial joints based on the range of motion.
i. Ball-and-socket joint allow motion in all directions e.g., shoulder and hip joints.
ii. Hinge joint allow movement in only one plane, like a door hinge e.g., elbow and knee
joints.
iii. Pivot joint allow rotational movement around a single axis e.g., joint between the first
(Atlas-C1) and second (Axis-C2) vertebrae of the neck.

--- Page 12 ---
iv. Ellipsoidal joint allow movement in two planes, but not rotation e.g., joint of wrist
with radius.
v. Saddle joint allow movement in two planes because one bone has a concave surface
and the other has a convex surface e.g., thumb, sternoclavicular and incudomalleolar
joints (joint between malleus and incus of middle ear ossicles).
vi. Gliding (Plane) joint allow gliding movements between bones e.g., joints between the
vertebrae and the joints between the bones in wrist (inter-carpal) and ankle (inter-tarsal).
★Q8. What is joint transplantation/Arthroplasty? Describe most common types of
joint transplantation.
Ans. Joint Transplantation: It is a surgical procedure in which a damaged joint is
replaced with a healthy natural joint (from donor) or an artificial joint.
Types: The most common types of joint transplantation are:
1. Total arthroplasty / Total joint replacement: In this procedure, the entire damaged
joint is replaced with an artificial joint made of metal, plastic, or ceramic.
2. Partial arthroplasty / Partial joint replacement: In this procedure, only the damaged
part of the joint is replaced with an artificial component. This is often used in the knee
joint.
3. Allograft transplantation: In this procedure, a healthy joint from a donor is
transplanted to replace the damaged joint. This technique is often used in the ankle and
knee joints.
4. Chondrocyte implantation: In this procedure, chondrocytes from patient's own
joint are implanted into the damaged joint. This technique is often used in the knee
joint.
★Q9. How the bipedal posture of humans is linked to skeleton and musculature?
Which problems can arise due to improper posture?
Ans. Human Skeleton & Musculature helps in Bipedal Posture
(a) The bipedal posture of humans is linked to skeleton and
musculature in several ways.
• S-Shaped Vertebral Column: The human vertebral column
has a distinctive S-shaped curve, which helps to distribute
weight evenly and maintain balance while standing and
walking.
• Broad and Short Pelvis: Human pelvis is shorter and
broader, which helps to stabilize the torso (body excluding the
head, neck and limbs, also called trunk) and support the
body's weight on two legs.
• Angled Femur: The human femur is also angled inward
towards the knee joint, which helps to keep the body's centre
of mass over the feet. It allows stability while standing and
walking.
• Gluteal Muscles: The muscles are located in the buttocks
(gluteus maximus, gluteus medius and gluteus minimus), are
much larger in humans. They play a crucial role in stabilizing
the torso and propelling the body forward while walking.

iii. Muscle Imbalance: Overused and underused muscles from poor posture can pull bones
and joints out of alignment.

Q15. Describe the three types of muscles.
Ans. Definition: Muscle is defined as the tissue that can contract in a coordinated way to
produce movements of body parts or whole body. The individual cells of muscle are called
muscle fibres or myofibres or
myocytes.
Types of Muscles: Human body has
three types of muscle tissues: skeletal,
smooth, and cardiac.
i. Skeletal Muscles: Skeletal
muscles are responsible for
moving parts of the body, such
as the limbs, trunk, and face. The
muscle fibres of skeletal muscles
are elongated cells with striations
have many nuclei per cell.
Because their contractions are
usually consciously controlled,
skeletal muscles are called as
voluntary muscles.
ii. Smooth Muscles: Smooth
muscles are present in the walls of
the stomach, intestines, blood
vessels, and other internal organs.

--- Page 18 ---
Smooth muscle fibres are spindle-shaped, have a single nucleus and lack striations.
Smooth muscle fibres are surrounded by connective tissue. Because most of their
movements cannot be consciously controlled, smooth muscle is referred to as
involuntary muscle.
iii. Cardiac Muscles: These are found only in the walls of the heart (myocardium). Their
fibres branch extensively. The muscle fibres of cardiac muscles are striated like skeletal
muscle, but each cell usually contains one nucleus located near the centre and is
involuntary in control.

| Comparison of three types of muscle tissues | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Property** | **Skeletal Muscle** | **Smooth Muscles** | **Cardiac Muscles** |
| Appearance | Regular striped | Un-striped | Irregular striped |
| Cell shape | Spindle or cylindrical | Spindle | Branched |
| Number of nuclei | Many per cell | One per cell | One per cell |
| Voluntary control | Have voluntary control | Usually, no voluntary control | No voluntary control |
| Function | To move skeleton | To move substances through hollow organs | To pump blood |

Q16. Explain the ultrastructure of skeletal muscle.
Ans. Structure of Skeletal Muscles: The cells of skeletal muscles i.e., muscle fibres
(myofibres) are in the form of bundles which are enclosed by collagen fibres and connective
tissue. At the ends of a skeletal muscle, the collagen and connective tissue forms tendons
which attach the muscle to bones.
Ultrastructure of Skeletal Muscles: Each skeletal muscle cell i.e., muscle fibre is a
cylindrical multinucleated cell, enclosed by a plasma membrane called sarcolemma. Its
cytoplasm is called sarcoplasm (have organelles, enzymes and glycogen) and it contains
sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR), SER of skeletal muscles have stored Ca++ and no ribosomes.
The sarcolemma penetrates deep into the cell to form hollow elongated tubes, the
transverse tubules (T-tubules). The T-tubules reach the ends of SR.
Myofibrils: Each muscle fibre contains a bundle of 4 to 20 elongated threadlike
structures called myofibrils. Myofibrils are made up of two types of filaments.
1. Thick filaments composed of myosin. The thick filaments create dark bands called A-
bands.
2. The thin filaments are composed of actin. create light bands called I-bands. These
alternating dark and light bands give skeletal muscle its striped (striated) appearance.
• Z-lines: The thin actin filaments are attached to protein discs called Z-lines. The section
between two Z-lines is a sarcomere, the smallest unit of muscle contraction. Within a
sarcomere, the thin filaments extend from the Z-line toward the center. where they
overlap with thick filaments. This overlap creates the A-band, with a lighter central
region called the H-zone/H-band where no overlap occurs.

Q18. Write a detailed note on sliding filament model of muscle contraction.
Ans. Mechanism of Muscle Contraction - Sliding Filament Model
The sliding filament model explains how a muscle contracts. According to this model, a
muscle contracts when its thin myofilaments slide past the thick ones so that they overlap to
a greater degree.
Steps: It occurs in the following steps.
1. Sarcomeres at relaxed state: In a relaxed muscle, sarcomeres are at their normal
length. The myosin heads are not bound to actin because the binding sites on actin are
blocked by tropomyosin of thin filaments. Troponin, another protein, is attached to
tropomyosin. Myosin heads have hydrolysed ATP into ADP and Pi.
2. Arrival of Nerve Impulse: When a nerve impulse reaches the muscle fibre, it travels
along the sarcolemma to the T-tubules and then to the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR). The
SR releases calcium ions into the cytosol. These calcium ions bind to troponin, causing
it to shift tropomyosin away from the myosin-binding sites on actin.

• Binding sites on actin are blocked;
• Myosin head has hydrolysed ATP
into ADP and Pi.

• ATP attaches with myosin head;
• Myosin head detaches from actin.

• Ca ions bind with troponin;
• Binding sites on actin are open;
• Myosin heads attach with actin

• Myosin heads release ADP and Pi;
• Heads undergo conformational
change and pull actin filament
towards centre.

Figure: Steps of a power stroke (cross bridge cycle)

--- Page 21 ---
3. Cross-bridges and Power-stroke: When binding sites on actin are exposed, the myosin
heads bind to them and form cross-bridges. Once the cross-bridges are formed, the
myosin heads release the ADP and Pi, and undergo conformational change. They bend
towards the centre of sarcomere, pulling actin filaments with them. This pulling action is
called a power stroke.
It shortens the sarcomere, bringing Z-lines closer together and H-zone disappears. It
occurs simultaneously in all sarcomeres, causing the muscle to contract. The adjacent A-
bands of sarcomeres come closer to each other but do not shorten.
4. Separation of Myosin Heads from Actin: After pulling, the myosin head receives a
new molecule of ATP. This allows the head to detach from actin. Splitting of this ATP
into ADP and Pi puts the head into its original conformation, allowing the cross-bridge
cycle to begin again.
Q19. Elaborate the arrangement of skeletal muscles of moveable joints to aid various
movements. / Describe the antagonistic arrangement of skeletal muscle with examples.

Ans. Skeletal muscles are attached to bones by tough connective tissues called tendons.
Parts of structural muscle: Typically, a muscle has two attachment points on different
bones. The end attached to the stationary bone during contraction is called the origin, while
the end attached to the bone that moves is the insertion. The middle part of the muscle is
known as the belly.
Antagonism: For the movement of bones at a joint in two directions muscles work in pairs.
They produce opposing actions when they contract. Such arrangement of muscles is called
antagonistic arrangement.
Flexor: The muscle which bends the bone at joint upon contraction is called flexor.
Extensor: The muscle which straightens the bone at joint upon contraction is called
extensor. During such antagonistic action, when a muscle e.g., flexors contracts, the other
muscle i.e., extensor is relaxed and vice versa.
• Movement at Knee Joint as an example of antagonistic movement: The knee joint is
located between the femur (thigh bone) and the tibia and fibula (lower leg bones).
Flexion: Flexion, or bending, of the lower leg is done by the hamstrings. It is a group of
three muscles at the back of the thigh.
Origin of hamstrings: The hamstrings originate at the pelvic girdle and the top of the
femur.
Insertion of hamstrings: It is inserted at the upper parts of the fibula and tibia.
Extensions: Extension, or straightening, of the lower leg is done by the quadriceps. It is a
group of four muscles at the front of the thigh.
Origin of Quadriceps: The quadriceps originate at the ilium (part of the pelvic girdle) and
femur.
Insertion of quadriceps: It is inserted at the patella (knee cap) and tibia. When the hamstrings
contract, the lower leg bends and the quadriceps relax. When the quadriceps contract,
the lower leg straightens and the hamstrings relax.

--- Page 22 ---
Q20. Describe causes and symptoms of muscle fatigue, cramps and tetany.
Ans. Muscle Disorders: The following are some common muscle disorders
1. Muscle Fatigue: Muscle fatigue means a decline in muscle performance that occurs
after prolonged or intense physical activity or due to some disease.
Causes: The following factors contribute to muscle fatigue:
i. Low ATP: During exercise, the muscles use ATPs to contract. When the supply of ATPs
is depleted, the muscle is no longer able to contract.
ii. Metabolic Waste: As muscles work, they produce metabolic wastes e.g., lactate,
hydrogen ions, and reactive oxygen. These wastes contribute to muscle fatigue.
iii. Ca++ ion handling: When muscle fibres are repeatedly activated, they are not able to
effectively handle calcium ions, which can impair muscle function.
iv. Damage to muscle fibres: Prolonged or intense exercise can cause small amounts of
damage to muscle fibres, leading to inflammation and reduced muscle function.
Symptoms: Its symptoms include pain, decreased muscle strength, and reduced
endurance. Muscle fatigue typically improves with rest. If it is severe, it requires medical
attention.
2. Muscle Cramps
Muscles cramps are sudden, involuntary and often painful contractions of a muscle or
group of muscles. They usually last from a few seconds to several minutes and most
commonly occur in the legs and feet.
Causes
i. Dehydration
ii. Imbalance of salts
iii. Overuse or injury of the muscle
iv. Medications (like diuretics)
v. Medical conditions such as diabetes
vi. Liver disease
vii. Nerve damage
Treatment: To relieve muscle cramps, gently stretch and massage the affected muscle.
Applying heat or cold to the area and using pain-relieving medications can also help.
3. Tetany
Tetany is a condition characterized by involuntary muscle contractions or spasms due to
increased muscle tone and hyperexcitability of the nerves. These contractions can occur
in various parts of the body such as hands, feet, face or larynx.
Causes
(i) The most common cause of tetany is hypocalcaemia (low level of calcium in blood)
which may be due to vitamin D deficiency.
(ii) Renal failure or thyroid disorders.
(iii) Salts imbalances, such as low level of magnesium in blood.
Treatment: Treatment for tetany depends on the underlying cause. If tetany is caused by
salts imbalances, treatment may involve calcium or magnesium supplements or intravenous
fluid to restore electrolyte balance.

Difference between Tetany and Tetanus
| Tetany | Tetanus |
| :--- | :--- |
| • Tetany involves increased muscles tone and overactive nerves, causing involuntary muscle creations or spasms. | • Tetanus is a severe bacterial infection caused by Clostridium tetani, which produces a toxin affecting the nervous system, leading to muscle stiffness and spasms. |
| • Tetany can affect various body parts like the hands, feet, face or larynx. | • Tetanus mainly affects the jaw and neck muscles. |
| • Tetany can result from issues like electrolyte imbalances or nerve problems. | • Tetanus is caused by a specific bacterial infection. |
| • Tetany is less serious and usually not life-threatening as compared to tetanus. | • Tetanus is more serious and potentially life-threatening compared to tetany. |

★Q20.Justify how the main functions of the skeleton are to act as a system of rods and levers.
Ans. Skeleton is a system of rods and levers: The skeleton works like a system of rods and levers. Bones act as the rods, giving structure and support to the body and protecting internal organs.
In this system, joints serve as fulcrums (pivot points) for the levers, allowing movement. Muscles generate the effort or force, while the weight or resistance being moved is the load.
For example, when lifting a weight, the bicep muscle in the upper arm acts as a lever. The elbow joint is the fulcrum, the bicep provides the effort, and the weight is the load.
★Q21.Justify why do muscles pull but don't push?
Ans. Muscles can only pull: Muscles can only pull, not push. This is because muscle fibres are designed to contract and shorten, pulling on tendons and thus moving bones.
When a muscle contracts, it pulls on the bone via the tendon, and when it relaxes, the bone moves back to its original position.
Muscles cannot push because they only generate force by pulling. If a muscle were to push, it would need to be attached to bones at both ends and make both ends move closer together,
which is not possible in the body. Muscles are usually attached to bone at only one end.

Unit 12: Human Skeletal and Muscular Systems

Short Questions

SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS EXERCISE

Q.1 Name three types of cells
associated with bone and write their
functions.

Ans. Types of Bone Cells

There are three types of cells i.e.,
osteoblasts, osteocytes, and osteoclasts
involved in the development, growth and
remodelling of bones.

1. Osteoblasts are bone forming cells that
synthesize and secrete unmineralized
ground substance. Once the osteoblasts
are surrounded by matrix, they become
the osteocytes.

2. Osteocytes are mature bone cells which
maintain healthy bone tissue by
secreting enzymes and bone mineral

[REPORT ANY MISTAKE AT: FREEILM786@GMAIL.COM] [WEBSITE: WWW.FREEILM.COM]

--- Page 2 ---
content. They also regulate the calcium
release from bone tissue to blood.
3. Osteoclasts develop from macrophages
and are involved in bone resorption, i.e.,
they break down bone and release
calcium and phosphate in blood.
Osteoblasts
(form bone matrix)
Osteoclast
(resorbs bone)
Osteogenic cell
(stem cell)
Osteocyte
(mature bone cell)
Q.2 Name the bones of cranium.
Ans. Eight cranial bones form cranium
also called brain box.
i. Paired bones: Two paired bones,
parietal and temporal.
ii. Unpaired bones: Four unpaired bones,
Frontal, occipital, ethmoid and sphenoid.
Q.3 Enlist the bones in the five groups
of vertebrae.
Ans. Vertebral column: It consists of 33
vertebrae. The vertebrae make five groups:
i. Seven cervical vertebrae: These are the
vertebrae of the neck. The first one is
called atlas and the second one is called
axis.
ii. Twelve thoracic vertebrae: These are
rib-carrying vertebrae and are found in
chest region.
iii. Five lumbar vertebrae: These are
present in abdominal region.
iv. Five sacral vertebrae: These are five
fused vertebrae forming the sacrum. The
sacrum articulates with the iliac bones of
the hip to form the back of the pelvis.
v. Four coccygeal vertebrae or coccyx:
These vertebrae are fused in the adults.
Sacral and coccygeal vertebrae are
together called pelvic vertebrae.
Q.4 What bones make the rib cage?
Ans. The rib cage consists of 24 bones (12
pairs) called ribs and a sternum. The
sternum (chest bone) is a long flat bone
located in the central part of the chest. The
ribs articulate posteriorly with the thoracic
vertebrae.
True ribs: On anterior side, first 7 pairs of
ribs attach directly with the sternum by
means of separate costal cartilages. These
are called true ribs.
False ribs: The 8th, 9th and 10th pairs
attach to the sternum by means of a common
costal cartilage and are called false ribs.
Floating ribs: The last 2 pairs of ribs (11th
and 12th) are known as floating ribs,
because they do not attach to the sternum.
Q.5 Name the bones of pectoral girdle
and pelvic girdle
Ans. Pectoral girdle: It consists of 2 pairs
i.e., a pair of clavicles (collar bones) and a
pair of scapulae (shoulder bones). One end
of each clavicle articulates with the sternum.
The other end articulates with the scapula.
Pelvic girdle: It is made up of two hip
bones. Each hip bone contains 3 fused bones
i.e., ilium, ischium and pubis. In each hip
bone, there is a bony socket, called
acetabulum that is formed by the fusion of
three bones. The two hip bones are joined at
the front by the pubic symphysis (a
cartilaginous joint that connects the pubic
bones at the midline of the body).
Q.6 Name the bones of forelimbs and hindlimbs.
Fore Limb
• One humerus
• One ulna and one radius
• Eight carpels
• Five meta carpels
• Fourteen phalanges
Hindlimb
• One femur
• One tibia and one fibula, one patella
• Seven tarsals
• Five metatarsals
• Fourteen phalanges

--- Page 3 ---
Q.7 What is fibrous joint? Give examples.
Ans. Fibrous Joints: In fibrous joints, the bones are directly connected to each other by fibrous connective tissue consisting mainly of collagen. These joints permit no movement of bones. Examples of fibrous joints include:
• Sutures that occur only between the immovable bones of the skull.
• Joints between the tibia and fibula bones in the lower leg.
• Joints between teeth and their sockets in the jawbone (mandible).
Q.8 Name the steps involved in bone repair.
i. Hematoma formation
ii. Soft callus formation
iii. Bony callus formation
iv. Remodelling
Q.9 Which skeletal structures are affected from the osteoarthritis?
Ans. Osteoarthritis is the most common chronic arthritic. It occurs when the articular cartilage at the ends of bones in joints gradually softens and disintegrates. It affects knee, hip and intervertebral joints.
Q.10 List the major parts of skeletal muscle fibre.
Ans. Each skeletal muscle cell i.e., muscle fibre is a cylindrical multinucleated cell, enclosed by a plasma membrane called sarcolemma. Its cytoplasm is called sarcoplasm and it contains sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR). The sarcolemma penetrates deep into the cell to form hollow elongated tubes, the transverse tubules (T-tubules). The T-tubules reach the ends of SR.
Q.11 What do you mean by I-band, A-band and H-zone?
I-Band: The thin filaments of myobril in a muscle cell create light bands called I-band (isotropic: they can't polarize light). These thin filaments are attached to protein discs called Z-lines (Zwishen: in between) They are composed of actin.
A-band: The thick filaments of myofibril in muscle fibre create dark bands called A-Band (Anisotropic: they can polarize light). They are composed of myosin.
H-zone: The region in A-Band which appears lighter (where no overlap between thick and thin filaments occur) is called H-zone (hele = bright).
Q.12 Describe the antagonistic arrangement of skeletal muscles.
Ans. For the movement of bones at a joint in two directions muscles work in pairs. They produce opposing actions when they contract. Such arrangement of muscles is called antagonistic arrangement. In such arrangement, when one muscle, called flexor, contracts it bends the bone at joint. When the opposing muscle, called extensor, contracts it straightens the bone at joints.
• During antagonistic action, when a muscle e.g., flexors contracts, the other muscle i.e., extensor is relaxed and vice versa.
Q.13 Ligaments are elastic while tendons are hard. Justify.
• Ligaments can stretch slightly under stress and retain to their original shape due to higher amount of elastin.
• Tendons are stiffer and resist stretching to efficiently transfer muscle forces due to higher collagen and relatively low elastin.

Q.15 Differentiate between:
• Compact and spongy bone
• Axial skeleton and appendicular skeleton
• True ribs, false ribs and floating ribs
• Rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis
• Fibrous and cartilaginous joints
• Cartilaginous and synovial joint

• Tropomyosin and troponin

Ans. Compact and spongy bone
| Compact bone | Spongy bone |
| :--- | :--- |
| • The outer thick layer of bone under the periosteum is called compact bone. | • The inner thin layer of bone under compact bone is called spongy bone. |
| • It is made of hard material. | • It is made up of latticework structure, consisting of bony spikes making it light and strong. |
| • It provides attachment and surface for muscles. | • It contains bone marrow so acts as a site for blood cells production. |

Axial skeleton and appendicular skeleton
| Axial skeleton | Appendicular skeleton |
| :--- | :--- |
| • The axial skeleton forms the axis of the body. Its bones support and protect the organs of the head, neck, and chest. | • Appendicular skeleton includes the bones present in appendages (arms and legs). |
| • It consists of skull, ribs, spine, and sternum. | • These are pectoral girdle, pelvic girdle, forelimbs and hind limbs. |

True ribs, false ribs and floating ribs
| True ribs | False ribs | Floating ribs |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| • The first seven pairs of ribs articulate directly with sternum by means of separate costal cartilages, these are called true ribs. | • The 8th, 9th and 10th pairs of ribs are attached to sternum by means of common costal cartilage, are called false ribs. | • The last 2 pairs of ribs 11th, 12th do not attach to the sternum, that's why they are called floating ribs. |

Rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis
| Rheumatoid Arthritis | Osteoarthritis |
| :--- | :--- |
| • It is result of an autoimmune disorder in which synovial membrane becomes inflamed. | • The type of arthritis in which articular cartilage at ends of bones in joints gradually softens and disintegrates. |

--- Page 5 ---
• Most commonly, the wrist and hands
are involved.
• It affects knee, hip and intervertebral
joints.
Fibrous and cartilaginous joints
Fibrous joints
• In fibrous joints, the bones are directly
connected to each other by fibrous
connective tissue consisting mainly
of collagen.
• These joints permit no movement of
bones. Examples of fibrous joints
include:
• Sutures that occur only between the
immovable bones of the skull.
Cartilaginous joints
• In these joints, the bones are connected
by a layer of cartilage.
• Cartilaginous joints allow little
movement of the bones.
• There are two main types of
cartilaginous joints:
(i) Primary cartilaginous joints
(synchondrosis)
(ii) Secondary cartilaginous joints
(symphysis)
Cartilaginous and synovial joint
Cartilaginous joint
• The type of joints in which, the bones
are connected by a layer of cartilage.
Cartilaginous joints allow little
movement of the bones.
• There are two main types of
cartilaginous joints:
• Primary cartilaginous joints
(synchondrosis): In some cartilaginous
joints, the bones are connected by hyaline
cartilage e.g., the joint between the first
rib and sternum
• Secondary cartilaginous joints
(symphysis): In some cartilaginous
joints, the bones are connected by
fibrocartilage e.g., pubic symphysis in
the pelvic girdle and intervertebral
discs.
Osteoblasts and osteocytes
Osteoblasts
• Osteoblasts are bone forming cells that
synthesize and secrete unmineralized
ground substance.
• Once the osteoblasts are surrounded by
matrix, they become the osteocytes.
Synovial joint
• Synovial joints are the most common
type of joint in the human body, and
they allow a wide range of movement.
• A smooth, tough, and elastic hyaline
cartilage, called articular cartilage,
covers the ends of the bones in the joint.
• It provides a smooth and frictionless
surface for movement.
• A fibrous capsule surrounds the
synovial joint.
• The fibrous capsule is composed of an
outer layer of ligaments and an inner
lining of synovial membrane, which
secretes synovial fluid, that lubricates
the joint.
Osteocytes
• Osteocytes are mature bone cells
which maintain healthy bone tissue by
secreting enzymes and bone mineral
content.
• They also regulate the calcium release
from bone tissue to blood.

Tropomyosin and troponin
| Tropomyosin | Troponin |
| :--- | :--- |

TnI = inhibitory polypeptide TnT = binds to tropomyosin TnC = binds calcium ions. |

Bone and Cartilage
Q.16 What are Haversian canals? Describe their components.
Haversian canal: the concentric layers of lamellae surround a central canal called the Haversian canal.
Components: It contains blood vessels, nerves and lymphatic vessels.
In addition to these structures, there are small channels that run perpendicular to the Haversian canals and connect them with each other and with the periosteum. Collagen fibres anchor the periosteum to the underlying bone tissue, providing additional strength and stability to the bone.

Q.18 What is bone marrow? Differentiate between red and yellow marrow.
Ans. Many bones contain a soft tissue called bone marrow, which can be either red or yellow.
• Red bone marrow is found in spongy bone, the ends of long bones, ribs, vertebrae, the sternum, and the pelvis. It produces red blood cells, platelets, and white blood cells.
• Yellow bone marrow fills the shafts of long bones. It consists of fat cells and serves as an energy reserve. It can also be converted to red bone marrow and produce blood cells when severe blood loss occurs.
Q.19 Define osteogenesis. Describe the formation of long bones.
Ans. Definition
• The process of bone formation is also called osteogenesis.
Formation
• It begins during embryonic development and continues throughout life, playing a vital role in growth, maintenance, and repair of bones.
• There are two primary pathways of osteogenesis.
• The formation of long bones e.g., femur and humerus, involves the transition of cartilage into bone. In this process, the center of cartilage begins to harden (calcify), and the chondrocytes (cartilage cells) in this area die, leaving behind cavities. Blood vessels penetrate these cavities and introduce osteoblasts and osteoclasts.
Q.20 Describe the formation of short bone.
• A few bones, e.g., some bones of the skull, develop directly into hard bone without forming cartilage first.
• In these cases, the osteocytes are initially scattered randomly throughout the embryonic connective tissue but soon fuse into layers and become flat plates of bones.
Q.21 Define Ossification.
Ans. The step in the formation of bone by which cartilage is replaced by bone by the deposition of minerals is called ossification.
★Q.22. Define periosteum, also describe the parts of bone.
• Periosteum: The bone's surface is covered by a tough layer of connective tissue called periosteum.
• Parts of bone: The broad ends of a bone are called epiphysis while the middle part along the length of bone is called diaphysis or shaft.

Q.28 What is fibrous capsule or joint
capsule? Give its composition.
Ans. A fibrous capsule surrounds the
synovial joint and helps to hold the bones
together. The fibrous capsule is composed of
an outer layer of ligaments and an inner
lining of synovial membrane, which secretes
synovial fluid, which lubricates the joint.
Q.29 Name the types of synovial joints
base on range of motion with one example
each.
Ans. There are six main types of synovial
joints based on the range of motion.
• Ball-and-socket joints allow movement
in all directions e.g., shoulder and hip
joints.
• Hinge joints allow movement in only one
plane, like a door hinge e.g., elbow and
knee joints.

--- Page 9 ---
• Pivot joints allow rotational movement
around a single axis e.g., joint between the
first and second vertebrae of the neck.
• Ellipsoidal joints allow movement in
two planes, but not rotation e.g., joint
of wrist with radius.
• Saddle joints allow movement in two
planes because one bone has a concave
surface and the other has a convex
surface e.g., thumb joint.
• Gliding joints allow gliding movements
between bones e.g., joints between the
vertebrae and the joints between the
bones in wrist and ankle.

Q.30 What is joint transplant? Describe
total and partial joint replacement.
Ans. Joint Transplantation
It is a surgical procedure in which a
damaged joint is replaced with a healthy
natural joint (from donor) or an artificial
joint. The most common types of joint
transplantation are:
Total joint replacement: In this procedure,
the entire damaged joint is replaced with an
artificial joint made of metal, plastic, or
ceramic.
Partial joint replacement: In this
procedure, only the damaged part of the joint
is replaced with an artificial component.
This is often used in the knee joint.

Q.31 Differentiate between allograft transplantation and chondrocyte implantation.
Allograft
• It is a type of joint transplantation in which
a healthy joint from a donor is
transplanted to replace the damaged joint.
• This technique is often used in the ankle
and knee joints.

Chondrocyte Implantation
• It is a surgical procedure, in which
chondrocytes from patient's own joint
are implanted into the damaged joint.
• This technique is often used in the knee
joint.

tears or ruptures, causing the inner gel-
like substance to leak out and press

include pain, numbness, and tingling in

Q.37 Characterize Gout.

• The most common joint affected is the

• Other joints (knees, wrists and fingers)

Q.38 What will be your most likely
diagnosis of a women of 60 years age
presenting with pain in legs, her lab tests
show decreased bone density and low
levels of oestrogen? Name the disease and
its causes.
• It is most probably the case of
osteoporosis. Osteoporosis is a condition
characterized by weakened bones that are
more prone to fractures and breaks. It
occurs when bone density decreases,
making the bones fragile and porous. Its
causes include:
• As people age, bone mass naturally
decreases. But it can be more pronounced
in some individuals.
• In women, a drop in oestrogen levels after
menopause accelerates bone loss. Lack of
calcium and vitamin D in the diet can
impair bone health.
• Long-term use of corticosteroids, can
contribute to bone loss.
• Smoking and alcohol consumption can
also increase the risk of osteoporosis.
• Lack of weight-bearing exercise can lead
to weakened bones.
Q.39 Define bone dislocation. Write its

Ans. Bone dislocation is a medical term,
which refers to a condition in which the
bones in a joint are forced out of their
