GAS EXCHANGE IN PLANTS
Q4. Describe opening and closing of stomata as per starch-sugar hypothesis.
Ans. The opening of stomata is primarily regulated by guard cells. At night, when
photosynthesis ceases due to lack of light, stomata typically close to conserve water. However,
plants still respire taking in O2 and releasing CO2. The closure of stomata at night helps
minimize water loss through transpiration.
Multisensory Hydraulic valves
The guard cells function as multisensory hydraulic valves. Guard cells functions as
multisensory hydraulic values as they open and close in response of certain environmental
factors like light, CO2 and humidity. The two hypotheses which may explain the opening and
closing of stomata are strach sugar hypothesis and influx of K+ ion.
Starch sugar hypothesis
In 1856, German botanist H. Van Mohl proposed that guard cells in leaf epidermis are solely
responsible for photosynthesis, producing sugars during the day. As sugar concentration
increases in guard cells, the water potential drops. Water moves into guard cells causing them
to become turgid and open the stomata. At night, photosynthesis ceases and sugars are
converted to insoluble starch or used for respiration, leading to a decline in free sugars.
Consequently, water move out of guard cells and they lose turgor pressure. So, they become
flaccid and close the stomata. However, this mechanism does not fully explain the rapid turgor
changes in guard cells during stomatal movements.
Q5. Explain influx of K+ ion in regulation of opening and closing of stomata.
How does abscisic acid overrides the effect of light and CO2 in stomatal
movement?
Ans. Influx of K+ ion
According to this hypothesis the opening of stomata in plants is facilitated by the active
transport of potassium ions (K+) into guard cells, which reduces their osmotic potential. This
influx of K+ leads to water entering the guard cells through osmosis, causing them to become
turgid and open the stomata.
Role of blue light: Blue light enhances this process by acidifying the surrounding
environment, promoting K+ uptake and subsequent water absorption. At night, K+ passively

[REPORT ANY MISTAKE AT: FREEILM786@GMAIL.COM]                                     [WEBSITE: WWW.FREEILM.COM]

--- Page 5 ---
[WANT TO GET ALL SUBJECT NOTES: WWW.FREEILM.COM]                                                               [WEBSITE: WWW.FREEILM.COM]

diffuses out of the guard cells, resulting in water loss and causing the guard cells to become
flaccid, thereby closing the stomata.
★ Hormonal Involvement
Hormones are involved in stomatal movement in plants. At high temperature when leaf cells
start wilting, a hormone called abscisic acid, is released by mesophyll cells. This hormone
stops the active transport of K+ into guard cells, overriding the effect of light and CO2
concentration. So, K+ pumping stops and stomata close.

SUPPORT IN PLANTS
Q6. What is palisade tissue? Give its structure and role in photosynthesis.

Ans. Palisade tissue is primarily located just beneath the upper epidermis of the leaf. It
consists of elongated, tightly packed cells that are rich in. The arrangement of these cells is
organized to maximize light absorption and allowing plants to efficiently convert light energy
into chemical energy.
Carbon dioxide from the atmosphere diffuses into the leaf through the stomata. Once inside,
the gas travels through air spaces within the spongy mesophyll and then into the palisade
mesophyll cells, where it is used in photosynthesis. Oxygen produced during photosynthesis
diffuses out of the palisade cells back through the spongy mesophyll and exists the leaf
through the stomata.

Fig: Structure of a leaf showing cuticle, epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll,
guard cells and stomata.
Q7. Elaborate the role of different types of supporting tissues in plants.

Ans. Supporting tissues in Plants
Supporting tissues play an important role in maintaining the structural integrity, support
and flexibility of plants. These tissues consist of parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma,
xylem and phloem.
1. Parenchyma: The parenchyma tissue provides support to herbaceous plants and parts of
larger plants. The parenchyma cells of the epidermis, cortex and pith absorb water. This water
creates an internal hydrostatic pressure known as turgor pressure that maintains the rigidity of
cells.

[REPORT ANY MISTAKE AT: FREEILM786@GMAIL.COM]                                                               [WEBSITE: WWW.FREEILM.COM]

--- Page 6 ---
Role of Turgor Pressure: Turgor pressure arises from the elevated osmotic pressure within
the cell vacuole. The membrane that surrounds the vacuole is called the tonoplast. It has many
active transport mechanisms that move ions into the vacuole, even the elevated ionic
concentration, water is drawn into the vacuole, resulting in turgidity and providing mechanical
support to the plant's soft tissues.
2. Collenchyma: Collenchyma cells are specialized cells that are grouped in the form of
strands or cylinders. They are found beneath the epidermis of young stems, leaf stalks and
along veins in leaves. Collenchyma cells lack secondary walls. Their primary walls are
thickened at the corners, due to extra deposition of cellulose. They elongate when stem or leaf
grown lengthwise. They provide support to the young parts of plant in which secondary
growth has not taken place.
3. Sclerenchyma: This tissue provides structural support to the plants. Typically, the cells of
sclerenchyma tissue possess thick secondary cell walls. These walls are saturated with lignin,
an organic compound that gives strength and rigidity to the walls. The majority of
sclerenchyma cells are non-living. The main function of this tissue is to provide support to the
various components of the plant.

(ii) Sclereids are smaller in size as compared to fibers and are present in the seed coats and

                                 WATER POTENTIAL
Q8. What is water potential? Describe the effects of solute and atmospheric
pressure on water potential?
Ans. Water Potential (Ψw)
Water molecules possess kinetic energy which means that in liquid or gaseous form they
move about rapidly and randomly from one place to another. So, greater the concentration of
the water molecules in a system the greater is the total kinetic energy of water molecules. This
is called water potential (symbolized by Greek letter Psi =Ψw).
Pure water has maximum water potential which by definition is zero. Water moves from a
region of higher Ψw to lower Ψw. All solutions have lower Ψw than pure water and so have
negative value of Ψw (at atmospheric pressure and at a defined temperature). So the osmosis
can be defined as the movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential to
a region of lower water potential through a partially permeable membrane.
Factors that determine water potential
In plant cells, two factors determine water potential i.e., Solute potential (Ψs) and Pressure
potential (Ψp).
1. Solute Potential (Ψs)
The solute potential or osmotic potential is a measure off the change in water potential (Ψw)
of a system due to the presence of solute molecules. Ψs is always a negative value, so if more
solute molecules are present, lower (more negative) is the Ψs.
2. Pressure Potential (Ψp)
It is the part of water potential which is due to the pressure exerted by water. If pressure greater
than atmospheric pressure is applied to pure water or a solution, its water potential increases.
When water enters plant cells by osmosis, pressure may be build up inside the cell making the
cell turgid and increasing the pressure potential.
Thus, the total water potential (Ψw) is sum of solute potential (Ψs) and pressure potential (Ψp):
Ψw =Ψs +Ψp
If we use the term water potential, the tendency for water to move between any two systems
can be measured; not just from cell to cell in a plant but also from soil to root, from leaf to air
and from soil to air. The steeper the potential gradient the faster is the flow of water along it.
                          TRANSPORT OF WATER IN PLANTS
Q9. Which pathways are followed by water to reach xylem from soil?
Ans. Uptake of Water by Roots
Roots of plants provide large surface area for absorption by their extensive branching systems.
Roots have tiny root hairs, which are actually extensions of epidermal cells of roots. Most
of the uptake of water and minerals in roots takes place through root hairs.

[REPORT ANY MISTAKE AT: FREEILM786@GMAIL.COM]                                     [WEBSITE: WWW.FREEILM.COM]

--- Page 8 ---
From soil, water and minerals enter the root epidermal cells by active and passive transport.
From root epidermis, they move to cortex and then into the xylem tissue in the centre of root.
Pathways: Inside roots, water and minerals move in three different pathways to reach the
xylem.
1. The Apoplast Pathway
It is a continuous pathway that involves a system of adjacent cell walls in the plant roots. The
apoplast pathway becomes discontinuous in the endodermis in the roots due to the presence
of Casparian segments.
2. The Symplast Pathway
In symplast pathway, water and minerals move through interconnected protoplasts of root
cells. The protoplasts of neighbouring cells are interconnected through plasmodesmata
which are cytoplasmic strands that extend through pores in adjacent cell walls. The symplast
pathway is less important, except for minerals in the region of endodermis.

Plasmodesmata Tonoplast
[Image of cells with arrows]
Vacuole Cell wall Cytoplasm
apoplast pathway Symplast pathway Vacuolar pathway
Fig: Water movement through apoplast, symplast and vacuolar pathways

3. The Vacuolar Pathway
In Vacuolar pathway, water and minerals move through cell membranes, cytoplasm and
tonoplast (membranes of vacuoles) and vacuoles. They move from vacuole to vacuole and
bypass the symplast and apoplast pathways. Movement in vacuolar pathway is negligible.

b. Vessels are shorter and broader compared to tracheids. They are arranged in a linear
fashion, forming continuous channels. Perforation plates are present at the outer edges
of these structures, enabling efficient movement of water.
c. Xylem fibres are elongated cells with thickened lignified walls. At maturity, they are dead
and enhance the structural integrity of the xylem. They offer additional structural
support to the plant.
d. Xylem parenchyma are living cells with thin walls that have the ability to retain and hold
nutrients and water. Xylem parenchyma cells participate in the lateral translocation of
water and nutrients and can also contribute to the healing and regeneration of xylem tissue.
Q11. Explain the TACT mechanism of water flow from root to leaf?
Ans.
The movement of water within plants, from roots to leaves, occurs primarily through
specialized vascular tissue known as xylem.
TACT: The TACT (Transpiration, Adhesion, Cohesion, Tension) also called cohesion –
tension theory is a widely accepted model explaining how water moves against gravity
through the xylem to reach all parts of the plant. This mechanism depends on both physical
and chemical properties of water and the plant's interaction with its environment.
Components of TACT mechanism
1. Transpiration
Transpiration is the process by
which water evaporates from
the surface of plant leaves,
specifically through stomata.
As water vapour exits the leaf,
a negative pressure is
generated within the leaf
tissue. This negative pressure
creates a pulling force, drawing
water upward from the roots
through the stem and towards
the leaves. Transpiration,
therefore, acts as the primary
driving force behind water
transport in the xylem.
2. Adhesion: Adhesion is the
attraction between water
molecules and the walls of
the xylem vessels. Due to
this attraction, water
molecules stick to the walls of xylem vessels as they move upward. This property prevents
any break in the water column within xylem. Adhesion thus plays a crucial role in maintaining

--- Page 10 ---
the continuity of the water column, especially in tall plants where gravity exerts a significant
downward force on the water column.
3. Cohesion: Cohesion refers to the attractive force between water molecules themselves,
caused by hydrogen bonding. Water molecules within the xylem stick together, forming an
unbroken column from the roots to the leaves. This cohesive property of water ensures that
the "pull" initiated by transpiration at the leaf level extends down through the entire water
column.
4. Tension: Tension is the negative pressure created by the pulling force of the transpiration
at the leaf level. As water evaporates from the leaf surface, it creates a low-pressure area that
extends through the xylem. This tension pulls the cohesive water column upwards. Tension is
therefore vital for the continuous ascent of water within the xylem.
TRANSLOCATION OF FOOD IN PLANTS
Q12. Describe the structural composition of phloem.
Ans. Structure of Phloem
Phloem is a vascular tissue in plants responsible for the transport of organic nutrients,
particularly the products of photosynthesis, from the leaves to other parts of the plant where
they are needed or stored. The phloem is generally found on the outer side of both primary
and secondary vascular tissue in plants with secondary growth. The phloem constitutes the
inner bark.
Components: Phloem comprises of sieve elements, companion cells, phloem fibres and
phloem parenchyma.
1. Sieve Tube Elements or Cells: The
cells of phloem that transport sugars and
other organic material throughout the
plant are called sieve tube elements or
cells. Sieve tube elements have 'sieve
areas', which are the portions of the cell
where pores interconnect the sieve tube
elements.
Sieve Tube: Some of the sieve areas are
generally formed in end walls of sieve
tube elements where the individual cells
are joined together to form a longitudinal
series called a sieve tube.
2. Companion cells: Each sieve tube
element is associated with one or more companion cells. Sieve tube elements and companion
cells are in communication with each other by plasmodesmata. Companion cells supply ATP
and proteins to sieve tube elements as they lack nucleus.
3. Phloem parenchyma: Phloem parenchyma stores substances, such as sugars, resins, latex
and mucilage which are important for plant defence and moisture retention.
4. Phloem fibers: Phloem fibres are specialized sclerenchyma cell, which are elongated,
spindle shaped have thick walls. These are crucial in providing mechanical support and
strength to plant.

--- Page 11 ---
Q13. Explain mass flow hypothesis for the transport of sugars?
Ans. Mechanism of Translocation of sugars
The transport of sugars in plants takes place through phloem tissue. Passive theories of phloem
transport include:
1. Diffusion is far too slow, to account for the velocities of sugar movement in phloem,
which on the average is 1 meter per hour, while the rate of diffusion is 1 meter per eight
years.
2. Pressure flow theory: The pressure-flow theory, also known as the mass-flow
hypothesis, is the most widely accepted explanation for the transport of sugars in plants
through the phloem. This process of translocation moves sugar from the source (where
they are synthesized) to the sink (where they are consumed or stored). This theory was
proposed by Ernst Munch in 1930. This theory relies on the principle of osmotic pressure
differences between source and sink regions.
Steps: Following steps explain the pressure-flow theory:

Xylem phloem
higher
hydrostatic
pressure

bulk flow
of solution
lower
hydrostatic
pressure
companion cell
leaf
(source of sucrose)
plasmodesmata

companion cell fruit (sink for sucrose)

sucrose active transport of sucrose
Fig: The pressure flow theory

1. The glucose formed during photosynthesis in mesophyll cells, is used in respiration. The
excess of glucose is converted into non-reducing sugar i.e., sucrose.
2. Sucrose is actively transported from mesophyll cells to the companion cells of phloem.
From here, sucrose diffuses to sieve tubes, through plasmodesmata. So, the concentration
of sucrose in sieve tubes increases.
3. Due to higher sucrose (solute) concentration in sieve tubes, water moves into them by
osmosis from the nearby xylem of leaf. It results in an increase in the water potential at
the source end of sieve tubes.

--- Page 12 ---
4. At the sink end, sugar is actively unloaded from sieve tubes and water also follows by
osmosis. The exit of water lowers the water potential at the sink end. So, there is a higher
water potential at the source end while a lower water potential at the sink end.
5. The difference in water potential causes water to flow from source to sink. Since sucrose
is dissolved in water, it is carried along from source to sink along with water.

GROWTH IN PLANTS

Q14. What are growing points in plants? Explain the types of meristem and their
role in growth. / What is the role of meristem in growth of plants?
Ans. Growth in Plants
Growth in plants refers to a permanent increase in size, which can occur in various
dimensions such as height, width and mass. Throughout life, the plant adds organs such as
branches, leaves and roots. Its organs increase in size from the tips but the rate of growth is
not uniform throughout the body.
Growing points: In lower plants, the entire plant body is capable of growing, but in higher
plants, growth is limited to certain regions known as growing points.
These growing points consist of groups of cells, called meristems that are capable of
continuous cell division.
Types of Meristems
There are three types of meristems in plants that accounts for growth in plants. i.e., apical
meristem, intercalary meristem and lateral meristem.
1. Apical meristems are found at
the tips of roots and shoots. They
are primarily responsible for the
extension of the plant body.
These are perpetual growth
(continuous growth) zones found
and are responsible for the
increase in the number of cells at
the tips of roots and stems. They
play an important role in
primary growth.
2. Intercalary meristems are
separated from the apex by
permanent tissues. They are
situated at the bases of
internodes in many plants such
as grasses and play an important
role in the production of leaves and flower. These are temporary.
3. Lateral meristems are cylinders of dividing cells present along the peripheral regions.
They are responsible for growth in thickness of stems and roots. They are found in woody
plants and are crucial for secondary growth. There are two main forms of lateral
meristems; vascular cambium and cork cambium.

--- Page 13 ---
• Vascular cambium is located between the xylem and phloem and is responsible for the
production of secondary xylem and secondary phloem.
• Cork cambium is formed in the outer layer of stems and roots. This tissue produces cork
cells which replace the epidermis and forms the outer protective bark.
Q15. Define primary growth in plants? Describe the phases of primary growth
in plants?
Ans. Primary Growth
Primary growth is responsible for an increase in the length of the plants. It is facilitated by
the activity of apical meristems. Herbaceous plants generally display primary growth with
little secondary growth as compared to woody plants.
Phases: The process of primary growth in plants occurs in three phases.
1. Cell Division: The cells of apical meristems
undergo mitotic division and the number of
cells is increased. It happens at the tips of
apical meristems of root and shoot. The area
of apical meristem where cell division
occurs, is called zone of cell division. In this
zone, cells are non-vacuolated and small.
These cells have spherical nuclei in the
centre of cytoplasm.
2. Cell Elongation: After the formation of new
cells, their volume increases due to uptake of
water. Plasticity of cell wall increases and
wall pressure is reduced. It happens at a little
distance from the tips of apical meristems.
The area where cell elongation occurs, is
called zone of cell elongation. In this zone,
cells are vacuolated and large. They have
nuclei in the peripheries of cytoplasm.
During this phase, different cells elongate in
different dimensions and the final size of
cells is attained. For example, the cells which are determined to develop into pith, cortex
etc. do not elongate much length-wise while the cells which are determined to develop
into xylem tissue elongate more length-wise.
3. Cell Differentiation: After the cells have got their final size and shape, elongation stops
and cells are specialized to perform specific functions. Their cell walls become thicker
and many new structural features develop. It happens in the area next to the zone of
elongation. In this zone, cells are fully differentiated and each type of cell performs
specific function.

Q16. Define secondary growth in plants. Describe the significance of secondary
growth in plants? / Describe the changes associated with change in season from
spring to autumn in cambium?
Ans. Secondary Growth
Secondary growth refers to the increase in thickness or girth of stems and roots. It is due to
the activity of lateral meristems, specifically the vascular cambium and cork cambium. It is
more prominent in woody perennial plants, while herbaceous plants show only primary
growth.

Annual Rings: Annual rings are formed due to the seasonal activity of the cambium layer in
trees. This process is influenced by environmental factors and results in the production of two
distinct types of wood each year spring wood (early wood) and autumn wood (late wood).
These rings provide valuable information about the age of the tree and the environmental
conditions experienced during each growing season.
• Cambium: The cambium is a meristematic tissue that generates new vascular tissues i.e.,
xylem and phloem.
• Growth in spring: In spring, when conditions are favourable, the cambium is highly
active, producing a large volume of xylem with wider vessels, resulting in lighter-coloured
spring wood.
• Growth in autumn: As the season changes to autumn, the cambium's activity
decreases. It produces fewer xylem elements, which are narrower and denser, leading to
the formation of darker autumn wood. The combination of spring wood and autumn
wood forms a complete annual ring. Each year, a new ring is added, allowing for the
determination of a tree's age through dendrochronology.
The transition between these two types of wood is gradual from spring to autumn, but the shift
from autumn back to spring in the following year is abrupt, marking a clear distinction
between the growth periods. This data is valuable for studying long-term climate variability
and changes.

PLANT GROWTH REGULATORS
Q17. What are plant growth regulators? Compare and contrast the roles of
auxins and gibberellins in plant growth.
Ans. Plant Growth Regulators
Plants regulate the rates of growth and the rate of metabolism in their cells. Special chemical
messengers, called plant growth regulators or plant hormones regulate their growth. There
are five major groups of plant growth regulators i.e., auxins, cytokinins, gibberellins,
abscisic acid and ethylene.
Auxins
• These are indole acetic acid (IAA) or its
variants.
• In stem, promote cell enlargement in
region behind apex.
• Promote cell division in cambium.
• In root, promote growth at very low
concentrations. Inhibit growth at higher
concentrations, e.g., geotropism. Promote
growth of roots from cuttings and calluses.
• Promote bud initiation in shoots but
sometimes antagonistic to cytokinins and
is inhibitory.
• Promote apical dominance and fruit
growth. They can sometimes induce
parthenocarpy.
• Cause delay in leaf senescence (aging) in
a few species.
• Inhibit abscission.
Gibberellin
• Gibberellins are produced in the apical
portions of roots and shoots, and
transported to other parts. Gibberellins
contain Gibberellic acid and there are
more than 110 different gibberellins.
• Promote cell enlargement in the presence
of auxins. Also promote cell division in
apical meristem and cambium.
• Promote ‘bolting’ of some rosette plants.
• Promote bud initiation in shoots of
chrysanthemum callus.
• Promote leaf growth and fruit growth.
May induce parthenocarpy.
• In apical dominance, enhance action of
auxins.
• Break bud and seed dormancy.
• Sometimes may substitute for red light.
Therefore, promote flowering in long-
day plants, while inhibit in short day
plants.
• Cause delay in leaf senescence in a few
species.
Q18. Cytokinins are one of the most important plant growth regulators,
comment.
Ans. Cytokinins
They are usually produced in roots, young fruits and in seeds. Cytokinins promote cytokinesis
during cell division. They increase the rate of DNA replication and the rate of RNA and
protein synthesis.
Functions: They perform the following:
• Promote stem growth by cell division in apical meristem and cambium.
• Inhibit primary root growth.
• Promote lateral root growth.

• Promote bud initiation and leaf growth.
• Promote fruit growth but can rarely induce parthenocarpy.
• Promote lateral bud growth, also break bud dormancy.
• Cause delay in leaf senescence.
• Promote stomatal opening.
Q19. What are the domains of actions of Abscisic acid and ethylene as growth
regulators in plants? / How Abscisic acid and ethylene effect plant growth during
physiological stress?
Ans. Abscisic acid
Abscisic acid (ABA) is synthesized mainly in mature green leaves, fruits and root caps.
Functions: It performs the following functions:
• Inhibits stem and root growth notably during physiological stress, e.g., drought and
waterlogging.
• Promotes bud and seed dormancy.
• Promotes flowering in short day plants and inhibits in long day plants (antagonistic to
gibberellins).
• Sometimes promotes leaf senescence.
• Promotes abscission.
• Promotes closing of stomata under conditions of water stress (wilting).
Ethylene
It is a natural product of the metabolism of plants. Inhibits stem growth, notably during
physiological stress.
Functions: It performs the following functions:
• Inhibits root growth.
• Breaks dormancy of bud.
• Promotes flowering in pineapple.
• Promotes fruit ripening.
OSMOREGULATION IN PLANTS
Q20. Define osmoregulation. Write the effects of various types of solutions on
cells.
Ans. Osmoregulation in Plants
Osmoregulation refers to the process by which an organism maintains a stable internal
equilibrium of water and dissolved substances, irrespective of the surrounding environmental
conditions.
Many marine organisms undergo osmosis without the requirement for regulatory systems
since their cells have the same osmotic pressure as that of the sea.
However, some organisms must actively acquire, retain or eliminate water or salts in order to
regulate their internal water and mineral balance.

--- Page 17 ---
Types of Solutions and their effect on living cells
1. Hypotonic solution: A solution having reduced solute concentration relative to the
intracellular environment of a cell. As a result, water enters the cell by osmosis resulting
in the swelling.

In hypertonic conditions:
Plasmolyzed
In isotonic conditions:
Flaccid
In hypotonic conditions:
Turgid
Fig: Effect of Hypertonic, Hypotonic and isotonic solution to plant cell

2. Hypertonic solution: A solution having high solute concentration relative to the
intracellular environment of a cell. As a result, water moves out of the cell which causes
the cell to shrink due to loss of water, a condition called plasmolysis.
3. Isotonic solution: A solution whose solute concentration resembles to the intracellular
environment of the cell. Net movement of water between the cell and its environment is
zero in this case leaving no effect on size or shape of the cell.
Q21. Describe osmoregulation in hydrophytes and mesophytes?
Ans. Osmotic Adjustments in Plants
Plants are distributed in different habitats of aquatic, moderate, severely dry terrestrial and
saline nature, thus termed as hydrophytes, mesophytes, xerophytes and halophytes,
respectively.
1. Hydrophytes are adapted to aquatic environments, including marine and freshwater
ecosystems, though specialized osmotic adjustment mechanism, these are of two types.
• Marine hydrophytes thrive in saline (hypertonic) conditions, where water tends to leave
their solutes like proline, glycine, betaine and sugars to retain water by increasing their
internal osmotic potential. The have thick cuticles which further reduce water loss, and
they exhibit halophytic traits to tolerate high salinity e.g., seaweeds, seagrass, mangroves.
• Freshwater hydrophytes grow in hypotonic environments, where water continuously
enters their cells. These plants expel excess water through structures like hydathodes or
vacuoles to avoid overhydration (over flooding). They actively absorb essential ions, such
as potassium and calcium to maintain osmotic balance and compensate for the dilute
surroundings. With thin or absent cuticles, these plants facilitate water exchange and often
have reduced root systems relying on direct nutrient and water absorption form their
environment. Examples of hydrophytes are water lilies, lotus and tape grass.
2. Mesophytes live in moderate environments that are neither too dry nor too wet:
• They prefer soil that is not waterlogged and has a moderate salt content and humidity.
• Mesophytes have well-developed roots and shoots with a fully formed vascular system.
• They do not require any special adaptations to survive.
• Their leaves are flat, broad and green with stomata on the surface.
• Examples of mesophytes include rose, tomatoes and daisies.

--- Page 18 ---

and high salt concentrations respectively?
Ans.
1. Xerophytes are plants that are adapted to
survive in dry conditions.
Adaptations: They have special adaptations
to minimize water loss and store water. Plants
that store water are known as succulents.
• They possess fleshy stems that can store
water and used when needed.
• Xerophytes include waxy coatings on
leaves to reduce water loss, leaf dropping
during dry periods and leaf folding or
repositioning to absorb sunlight
efficiently. Examples of xerophytes
include thorn trees, desert marigold,
cacti and blue agave.
Fig: A xerophytic plant (cactus)
2. Halophytes: Halophytes are the plants which inhabit saline soil with high concentration of
salts like NaCl, MgCl2, MgSO4 or saline water. On such a substratum, only those plants can
grow which can tolerate a relatively high concentration of these salts.
Adaptations
• These plants have succulent leaves and sometimes the stem is also succulent.
• In certain cases, leaves are modified into spines.
• Examples of halophytes are sea arrowgrass and sea lavender.
THERMOREGULATION IN PLANTS
Q23. Describe the Physiological adaptation of plants to extreme conditions. How
do plants adjust their cell membrane composition and protein structures to
survive high and low temperatures?
Ans. Thermoregulation in Plants
Thermoregulation is a homeostatic mechanism in which organisms maintain their internal
body temperature despite variations in environmental temperature.
1. High Temperature
High temperature denatures the enzymes and damages the metabolism. Plants use evaporative
cooling to cope with high temperature.
• Hot and dry weather, however, causes water deficiency resulting in closing of stomata, thus
plants suffer in such conditions.
• Most plants have adapted to survive in heat stress as the plants of temperate regions face.
the stress of 40°C and higher temperature. The cells of these plants synthesize large
quantities of special proteins called heat-shock proteins. These proteins embrace
enzymes and other proteins thus help to prevent their denaturation.
2. Low Temperature
i. Non – Freezing Temperature: Low temperature, alters the fluidity of the cell membrane,
because lipids of the membrane become locked into crystalline structures, which affects the
transport of the solutes. The structure of the membrane proteins is also affected.

--- Page 19 ---
[WANT TO GET ALL SUBJECT NOTES: WWW.FREEILM.COM]                                     [WEBSITE: WWW.FREEILM.COM]

• Adaptations: Plants respond to cold stress by increasing proportion of unsaturated fatty
acids, which help membrane to maintain structure at low temperature by preventing
crystal formation. This adaptation requires time. Because of this reason, rapid chilling of
plants is more stressful than gradual drop in air temperature.
ii. Freezing temperature
Freezing temperature causes ice crystal formation. The confinement of ice formation around
cell wall does not affect as badly and plants survive. However, formation of ice crystals within
protoplasm perforates membranes and organelles hence killing the cells.
• Adaptations: The plants native to cold region such as oaks, maples, roses and other
plants have adapted to bring changes in solutes composition of the cells, which causes
cytosol to super cool without ice formation, although ice crystals may form in the cell
walls.

MOVEMENTS IN PLANTS
Q24. What are tropic movements in plants? Explain major types of movements
in plants?
Ans. Tropic movements
The growth movements in plants that are triggered due to an external stimulus, are
collectively called tropic movements or tropisms. Such movements occur as a curvature of
whole organ towards or away from stimuli such as light, touch, chemical, water and gravity.
Types: Following are the major types of tropic movements in plants:
1. Phototropism: It is the movement of part of plant, in response to stimulus of light and
is caused by the differential growth of part of a plant like stem or root. The tips of shoots
usually show positive phototropism while roots show negative phototropism.
2. Geotropism: It is the movement of plant parts in response to gravity. Roots display
positive geotropism and shoots negative geotropism.
3. Thigmotropism: It is the movement in response to stimulus of touch, for example
climbing vines. When they come in contact with some solid object, the growth on the
opposite side of contact increases and the tendril coils around the support.
4. Chemotropism: The movement in plants in response to some chemicals is called
chemotropism. For example, the sugary environment on the stigma of a flower induces
pollen tube to grow inside the pistil/carpel to reach the ovule.

PHOTOPERIODISM
Q25. Define photoperiodism. Classify flowering plants according to
photoperiodism.
Ans. Photoperiodism
The response to changes in day length that enables plants to adapt to seasonal changes in their
environment is termed as photoperiodism. Simply, it is response of plants to the length of
day and night.
Contribution of Garner and Allard
Effect of photoperiodism was first studied in 1920 by Garner and Allard. They studied that
tobacco plant flowers only after exposure to a series of short days. Tobacco plant naturally
flowers under same conditions, in autumn, but flowering could be induced by artificially
exposing to short days.

[REPORT ANY MISTAKE AT: FREEILM786@GMAIL.COM]                                     [WEBSITE: WWW.FREEILM.COM]

--- Page 20 ---
Classification on basis of effect of light period
With further studies they were able to classify flowering plants into long-day plants, which
require long days for flowering, short-day plants, which require short days for flowering and
day-neutral plants which flower without being influenced by photoperiod.
Effect of Dark Period
Later on, further studies indicated that it is really the length of the dark period which is
critical. Thus, short-day plants are really long-night plants. If they are grown in short days,
but the long night is interrupted by a short light period, flowering is prevented. Long-day
plants will flower in short days if the long night period is interrupted.
Classification of plants according to photoperiodic requirements for flowering with
examples.
| Short-day plants (SDPs) | Long-day plants (LDPs) | Day-neutral plants (DNPs) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Flowering induced by dark periods longer than a critical length, e.g., cocklebur 8.5h; tobacco 10-11h. | Flowering induced by dark periods shorter than a critical length, e.g., henbane 13h. | Flowering independent of photoperiod. |
| Examples include cocklebur (Xanthium), chrysanthemum, soyabeans, tobacco, strawberry. | Examples include henbane (Hyoscyamus niger), snapdragon, cabbage, spring, wheat, spring barley | Examples include cucumber, tomato, garden pea, maize, cotton. |

Q26. Explain the role of Phytochrome in flowering.
Ans. Role of Phytochrome in flowering: Phytochrome a photoreceptor protein exists in
two forms i.e., P660 and P730, P660 is a quiescent form. It absorbs red light at a wavelength of
660 nm and is converted to active P730 which absorbs far red light at 730 nm and is converted
to P660.
In nature, the P660 to P730 conversion takes place in day light and P730 to P660 conversion occurs
in the dark.
The rate at which P730 is converted to P660 provides the plant with a “clock” for measuring the
duration of darkness.
It has been found that red light inhibits flowering in short-day plants but promotes flowering
in long-day plants, under conditions during which flowering normally takes place.
This observation led to the hypothesis that the P730 to P660 interconversion might be the plant
time-regulator for flowering.
According to this hypothesis, P730, converted from P660 by the absorption of red light would
inhibit flowering in short day plants but promote flowering in long day plants.
Because P730 accumulates in the day and diminishes at night, short day plants could flower
only if the night were long enough, during which a great amount of P730 would not be
completely inactivated, so that enough P730 would remain at the end of night to promote
flowering.
But now it is generally agreed that the time measuring phenomenon of flowering is not totally
controlled by the interconversion of P660 to P730.
Role of Florigen in flowering
Other factors, like presence or absence of light and length of dark or light period also play an
important role in flowering. The biological clock once stimulated causes production of

--- Page 21 ---
[WANT TO GET ALL SUBJECT NOTES: WWW.FREEILM.COM]                                     [WEBSITE: WWW.FREEILM.COM]

florigen hormone in leaves, which travels through phloem to the floral buds, initiating
flowering.

VERNALISATION
Q27. What is vernalisation? Describe its significance?
Ans. Vernalisation
The process of induction of flowering in plants by exposing them to certain low (chilling)
temperature is called vernalisation. It is usually effective in biennial and perennial plants.
Low Temperature
The low temperature stimulus is received by the shoot apex of a mature stem or embryo of
the seed but not by the leaves as in photoperiodism.
For some plants, vernalisation is an absolute requirement while in some cases it simply
assists in inducing flowering.
Duration: The duration of low temperature (chilling) treatment required varies from four
days to three months.
Temperature around 4°C is found to be very effective in this regard.
Significance
• It stimulates the production of a hormone “vernalin” which induces vernalisation.
• Photoperiodism and vernalisation serve to synchronise the reproductive behaviour of
plants with their environment, ensuring reproduction at favourable times of year.
• They also ensure that members of the same species flower at the same time, encouraging
cross pollination for genetic variability.

Unit 8: Plant Physiology

Short Questions

SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS EXERCISE

Q1. Differentiate between macronutrients
and micronutrients in plants?
| Macronutrients | Micronutrients |
| :--- | :--- |
| • Macronutrients are needed in relatively larger amounts in plants for growth and development. | • Micronutrients are needed in very smaller amounts in plants for growth and development. |
| • There are nine macronutrients in plants i.e., carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, potassium, calcium, phosphorus, magnesium and sulphur. | • There are seven micronutrients i.e., iron, manganese, zinc, molybdenum, copper, chlorine and boron. |

Q2. What is water potential?
Ans. Water molecules possess kinetic energy
which means that in liquid or gaseous form they
move about rapidly and randomly from one
place to another. So, greater the concentration of
the water molecules in a system the greater is the
total kinetic energy of water molecules. This is
called water potential psi = Ψw.
Factors: In plant cells, two factors determine
water potential i.e., Solute potential (Ψs) and
Pressure potential (ΨP).
Pure water has maximum water potential which
by definition is zero. Water moves from a region
of higher Ψw to lower Ψw.

Q3. What are the main three pathways
for the movement of water between plant
cells?
Ans. 1. The Apoplast Pathway
It is a continuous pathway that involves a
system of adjacent cell walls in the plant
roots. The apoplast pathway becomes

--- Page 2 ---
discontinuous in the endodermis in the roots
due to the presence of Casparian segments.
2. The Symplast Pathway
In symplast pathway, water and minerals move
through interconnected protoplasts of root cells.
The protoplasts of neighbouring cells are
interconnected through plasmodesmata, which
are cytoplasmic strands that extend through
pores in adjacent cell walls. The symplast
pathway is less important, except for minerals in
the region of endodermis
3. The Vacuolar Pathway
In vacuolar pathway, water and minerals move
through cell membranes, cytoplasm and
tonoplast (membranes of vacuoles) and
vacuoles. They move from vacuole to vacuole
and bypass the symplast and apoplast pathways.
Movement in vacuolar pathway is negligible.
Q4. Differentiate between hypertonic and hypotonic solution.
Hypotonic Solution
• A solution having reduced solute
concentration relative to the intracellular
environment of a cell.
• As a result, water enters the cell by
osmosis resulting in the swelling.
Hypertonic Solution
• A solution having high solute
concentration relative to the intracellular
environment of a cell.
• As a result, water moves out of the cell
which causes the cell to shrink due to loss
of water, a condition called plasmolysis.
Q5. What are halophytes?
Ans. Halophytes are the plants that inhabit
in saline soil with high concentrations of salts
like NaCl, MgCl2, MgSO4, or saline water. On
such a substratum, only such plants can grow
which can tolerate a relatively high
concentration of these salts.
Succulent leaves: These plants have succulent
leaves and sometimes the stem is also
succulent. In certain cases, leaves are
modified into spines.
Examples of halophytes are sea arrow grass
and sea lavender

plants and short day plants?
Short-day plants

flowering induced

longer than a

shorter than a

henbane 13h.

Q7. Write down the phases of plant
growth?
Ans. 1. Cell Division: The cells of apical
meristems undergo divisions and the number
of cells is increased.
2. Cell Elongation: After the formation of
new cells, their volume increases due to
uptake of water.
3. Cell Differentiation: After the cells have
got their final size and shape, elongation
stops and cells are specialized to perform
specific functions.

--- Page 3 ---
Q8. Differentiate between vernalin and florigen.
Vernalin
Florigen
Vernalin is a hormone which induces
vernalization which is a process in biennial
and perennial plants to stimulate flowering
by exposure to low temperature (4 days to 3
months).
Florigen is a hormone produced in leaves in
response to different concentration of P730;
it travels through phloem to floral buds
initiating flowering.
Q9. Differentiate between Thigmotropism and Geotropism?
Thigmotropism
Geotropism
• It is the movement in response to stimulus
of touch. When they come in contact with
some solid object, the growth on the
opposite side of contact increases and the
tendril coils around the support.
• For example climbing vines.
• It is the movement of plant parts in
response to gravity.
• For example, roots display positive
geotropism and shoots show negative
geotropism.
Q10. How intercalary meristem is different from apical meristem?
Apical Meristems
Intercalary Meristems
• Apical meristems are found at the tips of
roots and shoots.
• They are primarily responsible for the
extension of the plant body. These are
perpetual growth zones found and are
responsible for the increase in the number
of cells at the tips of roots and stems. They
play an important role in primary growth.
• The type of meristem situated at the base
of internodes.
• They are actually the part of apical
meristem, which are separated by
permanent tissues.
• Play an important role in the production
of leaves and flower, and are of temporary
nature.
SLO BASED SHORT QUESTION ANSWERS
Nutrition in Plants
Q11. Differentiate between nutrient and nutrition.
Nutrient
Nutrition
• A nutrient is a substance that provides the
body with essential ingredients required
for metabolism.
• Specific nutrients, such as carbohydrates,
lipids, and proteins, serve as sources of
energy.
• Nutrition refers to the collective processes
involved in the intake and utilization of
nutrients for growth, repair, and
maintenance of activities in an organism.
• It is of two types i.e. autotrophic and
heterotrophic nutrition.

--- Page 4 ---
• Other nutrients, including water,
electrolytes, minerals, and vitamins, are
necessary for the metabolic process.
Q12. What are the roles of Nitrogen and
Magnesium in plant? Also describe effects
of their deficiencies.
Ans. Role of Nitrogen
• Nitrogen is necessary for plant growth as
it plays an essential role in energy
metabolism and the production of proteins.
• Deficiency of nitrogen: A deficiency of
nitrogen results in leaf loss and stunted
growth.
Role of Magnesium
• Magnesium constitutes the core of the
chlorophyll molecule and is therefore
essential for photosynthesis.
• It promotes the absorption and
transportation of phosphorus and also
contributes to the storage of sugars within
the plant.
• Magnesium deficiencies result in weak
stalks, loss of greenness in the oldest
leaves, and the appearance of yellow and
brown spots.
Q13. Describe the roles of phosphorous
and potassium in plant growth.
Ans. Role of Phosphorus
• Phosphorus is a part of ATP. It also plays
a role in promoting root growth and favours
flowering in the aerial zone.
• Deficiency of phosphorus: A deficiency
of phosphorus leads to delayed flowering,
as well as the browning and wrinkling of
the leaves.
Role of Potassium
• Potassium is involved in water regulation
and the transportation of the plant's reserve
substances.
• It enhances the ability of plants to
carry out photosynthesis, reinforces
cellular tissue, and stimulates the uptake of
nitrates.
• Deficiency results in dark patches on the
leaves.
Q14. What are effects of deficiencies of
calcium and sulphur?
Ans. Effect of Calcium Deficiency
• Calcium provides stability to the cell wall
and promotes the development of the cell
wall.
• It also plays a role in cellular proliferation
and maturation, and aiding in the
development of seeds.
• Insufficient calcium leads to the
development of yellow and brown patches
on the leaves.
Effect off Sulfur Deficiency
• Sulfur is a fundamental element in the
metabolism of nitrogen.
• If there is a shortage of sulfur, the plant
becomes lighter in colour
Q15. How iron and manganese are
important to plants?
Ans. Importance of Iron
Iron is essential for the synthesis of
chlorophyll. It acts as a cofactor for several
enzymes which are involved in energy
transfer and nitrogen metabolism.
Deficiency: Its deficiency results in
interveinal chlorosis.
Importance of Manganese
Manganese is involved in the process of
photosynthesis, nitrogen metabolism,
carbohydrate metabolism and activation of
enzymes.
Deficiency: Its deficiency results in the
premature falling of the leaf and delayed
maturity.

--- Page 5 ---
Q16. How does zinc and molybdenum
are critical in plant growth?
Ans. Zinc
• Zinc facilitates chlorophyll synthesis, root
development and uptake of nutrients.
• Deficiency of zinc can lead to stunted
growth.
Molybdenum
• Molybdenum is critical for nitrogen
fixation, nitrogen reduction, sulfur
metabolism, phosphorus metabolism and
iron utilization.
• Deficiency: Its deficiency can result in
chlorosis of older leaves and stunted
growth.
Q17. How does zinc and chlorine
deficiencies manifest in plants?
Ans. Zinc
• Zinc facilitates chlorophyll synthesis, root
development and uptake of nutrients.
• Deficiency of zinc can lead to stunted
growth.
Chlorine
• Chlorine is involved in stomatal
regulation, osmotic adjustment and
transport of nutrients.
• Deficiency: Its deficiency can affect the
health and growth of plants.
Q18. All insectivorous plants are true
autotrophs then why does they capture
insects?
Ans. Insectivorous plants supplement
organic molecules into their food in
addition to inorganic nutrients, acquired
through the process of capturing and
breaking down insects and tiny animals.
• All insectivorous plants are true
autotrophs. However, their
development accelerates when they
capture prey.
• Apparently, nitrogenous compounds of
animal body are of benefit to these plants.
The captured insects are broken down by
enzymes that are released by the leaves.
• Pitcher plant, venus fly trap and sundew
are some of the known insectivorous
plants.
Q19. How does pitcher plant kill insects?
Ans. Pitcher plant has leaves modified
into a sac or a pitcher, partly filled with water.
• The leaf's terminal portion is altered to
create a hood, which partially covers the
exposed opening of the pitcher.
• It has numerous stiff hairs that prevent
little insects from crawling out once they
fall inside it.
Q20. How does venous fly trap is
adapted to fulfil its nitrogen
requirements?
Ans. Venus-fly trap has a "trap" consisting
of two lobes that are hinged at the end of each
leaf. The inner surfaces of the lobes contain
trichomes, which are hair-like projections
that trigger the lobes to close rapidly upon
contact with prey.
• The hinged traps are lined with fine
bristles that interlock upon closure,
preventing the prey from escaping.
• The trapped insect is then digested by the
enzymes secreted from the glands on the
leaf surface and the products are then
absorbed.
Q21. Which plants use/release odour to
trap its prey?
Ans. Sundew catches its prey with shiny
drops of "dew," where the plant's common
name comes from. The leaves are covered
with tiny hairs that look like tentacles.
• Each leaf has gland and has a single dew
like drop at the tip.
• The insects, attracted by plant's odour are
trapped by tentacles.
• The trapped insects are digested by
enzymes and products are absorbed.

Gas Exchange in Plants
Q22. Define stomata. Write their function.
Ans. Stomata are tiny opening or pores
present within the plant tissues which are
necessary for gaseous exchange.
• These are typically found in leaves but
can even be present in some stems.
• The stomata are surrounded by
specialized cells or the guard cells that
facilitate the opening and closing of the
stomatal pores.
• Guard cells are bean-shaped and contain
chloroplasts.
• Guard cells can open and close depending
on environmental conditions. The
opening and closing of stomata control
the transpiration rate in plants.
Q23. How are stomata involved in
gaseous exchange?
• During daylight stomata open to allow
CO2 to enter the plant for photosynthesis.
The opening of stomata is primarily
regulated by guard cells.
• At night when photosynthesis ceases due
to lack of light, stomata typically close to
conserve water. However, plants still
respire, taking in O2 and releasing CO2.
The closure of stomata at night helps to
minimize water loss by transpiration.
Q24. Guard cells function as
multisensory hydraulic valves justify.
Ans. Guard cells functions as multisensory
hydraulic values as they open and close in
response of certain environmental factors like
light, CO2 and humidity.
• They change shape due to water potential
and release excess water through
transpiration.

Q25. Brief about starch sugar
hypothesis.
Ans. Starch Sugar Hypothesis
In 1856, German botanist H. Van Mohl
proposed that guard cells in leaf epidermis are
solely responsible for photosynthesis,
producing sugars during the day. During day
time as sugar concentration increases in
guard cells, the water potential drops.
• Water moves into guard cells causing
them to become turgid and open the
stomata.
• At night, photosynthesis ceases, and
sugars are converted to insoluble starch or
used for respiration, leading to a decline
in free sugars. Consequently, water
moves out of guard cells and they lose
turgor pressure. So, they become flaccid
and close the stomata.
Q26. How does K+ ions facilitate opening
and closing of stomata? Also describe role
of blue light in K-influx.
Ans. The opening of stomata in plants is
facilitated by the active transport of
potassium ions (K+) into guard cells, which
reduces their osmotic potential. This influx of
K+ leads to water entering the guard cells
through osmosis, causing them to become
turgid and open the stomata.
• Blue light enhances this process by
acidifying the surrounding environment,
promoting K+ uptake and subsequent
water absorption.
• At night, K+ passively diffuses out of the
guard cells, resulting in water loss and
causing the guard cells to become flaccid,
thereby closing the stomata.
★Q27. How does abscisic acid overrides
the effect of light and CO2 in stomatal
movements?
Ans. Hormones are involved in stomatal
movement in plants during stress conditions.
At high temperature when leaf cells start

wilting, a hormone called abscisic acid, is
released by mesophyll cells. This hormone
stops the active transport of K+ into guard
cells, overriding the effect of light and CO2
concentration. So, K+ pumping stops and
stomata close.
Q28. Describe the location of palisade
tissue. How the arrangement of their cells
maximize light absorption and gaseous
exchange?
Ans. Palisade tissue is primarily located
just beneath the upper epidermis of the leaf.
It consists of elongated, tightly packed cells
that are rich in chlorophyll. The arrangement
of these cells is organized to maximize light
absorption and allowing plants to efficiently
convert light energy into chemical energy.

Support in Plants
Q30. Define tonoplast. How does it
maintain turgor pressure / rigidity of
cells?
Ans. The membrane that surrounds the
vacuole is called the tonoplast. It has many
active transport mechanisms that move ions
into the vacuole, even when the concentration
within the vacuole is higher than that of the
surrounding fluid.
• Due to the elevated ionic concentration,
water is drawn into the vacuole, resulting
in turgidity and providing mechanical
support to the plant's soft tissues.

Q31. How does parenchyma provide
support in plants?
Ans. The parenchyma tissue provides
support to herbaceous plants and parts of
larger plants.
• The parenchyma cells of the epidermis,
cortex, and pith absorb water This water
creates an internal hydrostatic pressure
known as turgor pressure that maintains
the rigidity of cells.
Turgor pressure arises from the elevated
osmotic pressure within the cell vacuole.
Q32. Describe the role of collenchyma
tissue in context of support.
Ans. Collenchyma cells are specialized
cells that are grouped in the form of strands
or cylinders.
• They are found beneath the epidermis
of young stems, leaf stalks and along
the veins in leaves.
• Collenchyma cells lack secondary
walls.
• Their primary walls are thickened at the
corners, due to extra deposition of
cellulose.
• They elongate when stem or leaf grows
lengthwise. They provide support to the
young parts of plant in which secondary
growth has not taken place.
Q33. Sclerenchyma confer strength and
rigidity to the cell walls of plants.
Ans. Sclerenchyma
This tissue also provides structural support
to the plants. Typically, the cells of
sclerenchyma tissue possess thick
secondary cell walls.
• These walls are saturated with lignin,
an organic compound that confers
strength and rigidity to the walls.
• The majority of sclerenchyma cells are
non-living.
• The main function of this tissue is to
provide support to the various
components of the plant.

--- Page 8 ---
Q34. Name the types of sclerenchyma cells and describe their roles.
Ans. There are three types of sclerenchyma cells which are fibres, sclereids and vessels.
1. Fibers (Tracheids) are elongated and cylindrical in shape. They can be found either as compact bundles inside the xylem or as bundle caps.
2. Sclereids are smaller in size as compared to fibers and are present in the seed coats and shells of nuts. Their function is to offer protection.
3. Vessels (Tracheae) are long tubular structures that are joined end to end to form a long water conducting pipe in xylem.

Q35. Differentiate between solute potential and pressure potential.
Solute Potential | Pressure Potential

• The solute potential or osmotic potential is a measure of the change in water potential (Ψw) of a system due to the presence of solute molecules. | • It is the part of water potential which is due to the pressure exerted by water it is denoted by Ψp. If pressure greater than atmospheric pressure is applied to pure water or a solution, its water potential increases.
• Ψs is always a negative value, so if more solute molecules are present, lower (more negative) is the Ψs. | • When water enters plant cells by osmosis, pressure may be built up inside the cell making the cell turgid and increasing the pressure potential

Transport of Water in Plants
Q36. Describe the role of roots and root hairs for efficient transport of water from soil to xylem. Enroute water from soil to xylem.
Ans. Roots of plants provide large surface area for absorption by their extensive branching systems. Roots have tiny root hairs, which are actually extensions of epidermal cells of roots. Most of the uptake of water and minerals in roots takes place through root hairs.
From soil, water and minerals enter the root epidermal cells by active and passive transport. From root epidermis, they move to cortex, and then into the xylem tissue in the centre of root. Inside roots, water and minerals move in three different pathways to reach the xylem.

Components of Xylem Tissue

Q42. Transpiration act as the primary driving force behind water transport in xylem. Justify.
Ans. Transpiration is the process by which water evaporates from the surface of plant leaves, specifically through stomata. As water vapour exits the leaf, a negative pressure is generated within the leaf tissue.
• This negative pressure creates a pulling force, drawing water upward from the roots through the stem and toward the leaves.
• Transpiration, therefore, act as the primary driving force behind water transport in the xylem.

Q43. Compare the roles of different forces of attraction involved in transpiration. / Compare the roles of adhesive forces and cohesive forces in movement of water.
| Adhesion | Cohesion |
| :--- | :--- |
| • Adhesion is the attraction between water molecules and the walls of the xylem vessels. | • Cohesion refers to the attractive force between water molecules themselves, caused by hydrogen bonding. |

• Due to this attraction, water molecules
stick to the walls of xylem vessels as they
move upward. This property prevents any
break in the water column within xylem.
• Adhesion thus play a crucial role in
maintaining the continuity of the water
column, especially in tall plants where
gravity exerts a significant downward
force on the water column.

Q44. Tension is vital for the continuous
ascent of water within xylem justify.

Ans. Tension is the negative pressure
created by the pulling force of the
transpiration at the leaf level. As water
evaporates from the leaf surface, it creates a
low-pressure area that extends through the
xylem. This tension pulls the cohesive water
column upwards. Tension is therefore vital
for the continuous ascent of water within the
xylem.
Translocation of Food
Q45. What do you know about TACT
theory?
Ans. The TACT (Transpiration, Adhesion,
Cohesion, Tension) also known as cohesion-
tension theory, is a widely accepted model
explaining how water moves against gravity
through the xylem to reach all parts of the
plant. This mechanism depends on both
physical and chemical properties of water
and the plant's interaction with its
environment.
Q46. Enlist the structural components of
phloem.
Ans. Phloem comprises of four major
components
• Sieve elements
• Companion cells
• Phloem fibres
• Phloem parenchyma.

• Water molecules within the xylem stick
together, forming an unbroken column
from the roots to the leaves.
• This cohesive property of water ensures
that the "pull" initiated by transpiration at
the leaf level extends down through the
entire water column.

Q47. Write few lines about phloem
tissue?
Ans. Phloem Tissue
• Phloem is a vascular tissue in plants
responsible for the transport of organic
nutrients, particularly the products of
photosynthesis, from the leaves to other
parts of the plant where they are needed
or stored.
• The phloem is generally found on the
outer side of both primary and
secondary vascular tissue in plants with
secondary growth and constitutes the inner
bark.
Q48. Describe the importance of sieve
tube elements in transport of sugars.

Ans. The cells of phloem that transport
sugars and other organic material throughout
the plant are called sieve tube elements or
cells. Sieve tube elements have 'sieve areas',
which are the portions of the cell wall where
pores interconnect the sieve tube elements.
Sieve tube elements join to form long sieve
tube, which is used to transport food from
source to sink.
Q49. Which substances are stored in
phloem parenchyma?
Ans. Phloem parenchyma stores
substances, such as sugars, resins, latex, and
mucilage, which are important for plant
defence and moisture retention.

Translocation of Food in Plants
Q50. Which passive theories were proposed for transport in phloem? Which theory is most widely accepted?
Ans. Passive theories of phloem transport include: Diffusion and pressure flow theory.
The pressure-flow theory, also known as the mass-flow hypothesis, is the most widely accepted explanation for the transport of sugars in plants through the phloem. This process of translocation moves sugar from the source (where they are synthesized) to the sink (where they are consumed or stored). This theory was proposed by Ernst Munch in 1930. This theory relies on the principle of osmotic pressure differences between source and sink regions.

Growth in Plants
Q51. What are growth pattern in plants?
Ans. Growth in plants refers to a permanent increase in size, which can occur in various dimensions such as height, width, and mass.
• Throughout life, the plant adds organs such as branches, leaves, and roots. Its organs increase in size from the tips but the rate of growth is not uniform throughout the body.
Q52. What are meristems? Give their types.
Ans. In higher plants, growth is limited to certain regions known as growing points. These growing points consist of groups of cells, called meristems, that are capable of continuous cell division.
• There are three types of meristems in plants i.e., apical meristem, intercalary meristem and lateral meristem.

Q53. How intercalary meristem is different from apical meristem?
Apical Meristem
• The type of meristem that are found at the tips of roots and shoots.
• They are primarily responsible for the extension of the plant body. These are perpetual growth zones found and are responsible for the increase in the number of cells at the tips of roots and stems.
• They play an important role in primary growth.

Intercalary Meristem
• The type of meristem situated at the base of internodes.
• They are actually the part of apical meristem, which are separated by permanent tissues.
• Play an important role in the production of leaves and flower, and are of temporary nature.

Q54. Characterize lateral meristem. Describe its main forms.
Ans. Lateral meristems are cylinders of dividing cells present along the peripheral regions. They are responsible for growth in thickness of stems and roots. They are found in woody plants and are crucial for secondary growth.
• There are two main forms of lateral meristems; vascular cambium and cork cambium.
• Vascular cambium is located between the xylem and phloem and is responsible for production of secondary xylem and secondary phloem.
• Cork cambium is formed in the outer layer of stems and roots. This tissue produces cork cells which replace the epidermis and forms the outer protective bark.

Q55. Define primary growth. Name its
phases.
Ans. Primary growth is responsible for an
increase in the length of the plants. It is
facilitated by the activity of apical meristems.
Herbaceous plants generally display primary
growth with little secondary growth as
compared to woody plants.
The process of primary growth in plants
occurs in three phases.
1. Cell Division
2. Cell Elongation
3. Cell Differentiation
Q56. Describe the events of zone of cell
division.
• The cells of apical meristems undergo
divisions and the number of cells is
increased.
• It happens at the tips of apical meristems of
root and shoot. The area of apical meristem
where cell division occurs, is called zone of
cell division.
• In this zone, cells are non-vacuolated and
small. These cells have spherical nuclei in
the centre of cytoplasm.
Q57. Describe the changes associated
with cell elongation phase.
• During elongation phase volume of cell
increases due to uptake of water.
• Plasticity of cell wall increases and wall
pressure is reduced. It happens at a little
distance from the tips of apical meristems.
• The area where cell elongation occurs, is
called zone of cell elongation. In this zone,
cells are vacuolated and large. They have
nuclei in the peripheries of cytoplasm.
• During this phase, different cells elongate
in different dimensions and the final size of
cells is attained.
• For example, the cells which are
determined to develop into pith. cortex etc.
do not elongate much length-wise while
the cells which are determined to develop
into xylem tissue elongate more length-
wise.
Q58. What happens after the cells got
their final size and shape during primary
growth? / Describe the final changes in
plants during primary growth.
Ans. Cell Differentiation: After the cells
have got their final size and shape, elongation
stops and cells are specialized to perform
specific functions, thus is termed as phase of
cell differentiation.
• Their cell walls become thicker and many
new structural features develop.
• It happens in the area next to the zone of
elongation. This area is called zone of cell
differentiation.
• In this zone, cells are fully differentiated
and each type of cell performs specific
function.
Q59. Define secondary growth. Which
tissue/ cells are responsible for it?
Ans. Secondary growth refers to the
increase in thickness or girth of stems and
roots. It is due to the activity of lateral
meristems, specifically the vascular cambium
and cork cambium. It is more prominent in
woody perennial plants, while herbaceous
plants show only primary growth. The cells
of vascular cambium divide and produce new
cells on both of its outer and inner margins.
Q60. Secondary tissues cause increase in
plants thickness. Justify.
• Secondary tissues (particularly secondary
xylem) cause increase in plant's
thickness.
• The cells of vascular cambium divide and
produce new cells on both of its outer and
inner margins of vascular cambium make
secondary phloem while the cells

--- Page 13 ---
produced on its inner margins make
secondary xylem.
• Division in cork cambium produces cells
on both outer and inner sides. The cells
make new cork.
Q61. Define bark and annual rings.

Ans. Bark: The region of mature stem
outside of the vascular cambium, which
contains secondary phloem, cork cambium
and cork, is collectively called bark.
A concentric layer of wood formed each year
in woody plants is called annual ring. Annual
rings are formed due to the seasonal activity
of the cambium layer in trees. These rings
provide valuable information about the age of
the tree and the environmental conditions
experienced during each growing season.
Q62. What is cambium? Describe the
effect of seasonal changes on its activity
and formation of annual ring?
Ans. The cambium is a meristematic tissue
that generates new vascular tissues i.e.,
xylem and phloem.
• In spring: In spring, when conditions are
favourable, the cambium is highly active,
producing a large volume of xylem with
wider vessels, resulting in lighter-
coloured spring wood.
• In autumn: As the season changes to
autumn, the cambium's activity
decreases. It produces fewer xylem
elements, which are narrower and denser,
leading to the wood forms a complete
annual ring.
★Q63.Define dendrochronology and its
importance.
Ans. Dendrochronology is the scientific
method of dating and studying tree rings to
analyze past climate conditions and events.

Q64. What are plant growth regulators?
Name their five major groups.
Ans. Plants regulate the rates of growth
and the rate of metabolism in their cells.
Special chemical messengers, called plant
growth regulators or plant hormones
regulate their growth. There are five major
groups of plant growth regulators i.e., auxins,
cytokinins, gibberellins, abscisic acid, and
ethylene.
Q65. Describe some important roles of
Auxins/Indole Acetic Acid.
Ans. Auxin (IAA) is one of the most
important plant growth regulator it:
1. Promotes cell division in cambium.
2. In roots, promote growth at very low
concentrations. Inhibit growth at higher
concentrations, e.g., geotropism. Promote
growth of roots from cuttings and calluses.
3. Promotes bud initiation in shoots but
sometimes antagonistic to cytokinins and
is inhibitory.
Q66. Where are gibberellins produced?
Describe their important activities.
Ans. Gibberellins are produced in apical
portions of roots and shoots and transported
to other parts.
• Promote cell enlargement in the presence
of auxins. Also promote cell division in
apical meristem and cambium.
• Promote 'bolting' of some rosette plants.
• Promote bud initiation in shoots of
chrysanthemum callus.
• Sometimes may substitute for red light.
Therefore, promote flowering in long-day
plants, while inhibit in short-day plants.
Q67. Why are cytokinins important for
plant growth?
Ans. Cytokinins are usually produced in
roots, young fruits and in seeds.
Cytokinins promote cytokinesis during cell
division. They increase the rate of DNA
replication and the rate of RNA and protein

--- Page 14 ---
synthesis. They perform the following
functions:
• Promote stem growth by cell division in
apical meristem and cambium.
• Inhibit primary root growth.
• Promote lateral root growth.
Q68. Describe the effects of abscisic acid
on plant stem, roots flowering and
stomata.
Ans. Abscisic acid (ABA) is synthesized
mainly in mature green leaves, fruits and root
caps. It performs the following functions:
• Inhibits stem and root growth notably
during physiological stress e.g., drought
and waterlogging.
• Promotes bud and seed dormancy.
• Promotes flowering in short day plants
and inhibits in long day plants
(antagonistic to gibberellins).
Q69. How does Ethene/ethylene support
the plants during physiological stress?

Ans. It is a natural product of the
metabolism of plants. Inhibits stem growth,
notably during physiological stress.
• Inhibits root growth
• Breaks root growth
• Promotes flowering in pineapple
• Promotes fruit ripening.
Osmoregulation in Plants
Q70. Define osmoregulation. How
osmoconformers differ from
osmoregulators?
Ans. Osmoregulation refers to the process
by which an organism maintains a stable
internal equilibrium of water and dissolved
substances, irrespective of the surrounding
environmental conditions.
• Osmoconformers: Many marine
organisms undergo osmosis without the
requirement for regulatory systems since
their cells have the same osmotic pressure
as that of the sea are called
osmoconformers.
• Osmoregulators: Organisms must
actively acquire, retain, or eliminate
water or salts in order to regulate their
internal water and mineral balance are
called osmoregulators.
Q71. Define hydrophytes. How are
freshwater hydrophytes adapted to live in
water?
Ans. Hydrophytes: These are the plants
adapted to aquatic environments (marine and
freshwater) by specialized mechanisms of
osmotic adjustments.
Freshwater hydrophytes grow in hypotonic
environments, where water continuously
enters their cells.
• These plants remove excess water
through structures like hydathodes or
vacuoles to avoid overhydration.
• They actively absorb essential ions, such
as potassium and calcium, to maintain
osmotic balance and compensate for the
dilute surroundings.
• With thin or absent cuticles, these plants
facilitate water exchange and often have
reduced root systems, relying on direct
nutrient and water absorption from their
environment.
Examples of hydrophytes are water lilies,
lotus, seaweeds and tape grass.
Q72. How plants maintain osmoregulation
in moderate environments?
Ans. Mesophytes live in moderate
environments that are neither too dry nor too
wet.
• They prefer soil that is not waterlogged
and has a moderate salt content and
humidity.
• Mesophytes have well-developed roots
and shoots with a fully formed vascular
system.

--- Page 15 ---
[WANT TO GET ALL SUBJECT NOTES: WWW.FREEILM.COM]                                                               [WEBSITE: WWW.FREEILM.COM]

• They do not require any special
adaptations to survive.
• Their leaves are flat, broad, and green
with stomata on the surface.
• Examples of mesophytes include rose,
tomatoes, and daisies.
Q73. How plants are adapted to live in
dry conditions? / Describe the adaptations
in succulents to reduce transpiration.

Ans. Xerophytes are plants that are
adapted to survive in dry conditions.

• They have special adaptations to
minimize water loss and store water.
• Plants that store water are known as
succulents.
• They possess fleshy stems that can store
water and used when needed.
• Other adaptations in xerophytes include
waxy coatings on leaves to reduce water
loss, leaf dropping during dry periods,
and leaf folding or repositioning to
absorb sunlight efficiently.
• Examples of xerophytes include thorn
trees, desert marigold, and blue agave.

★Q75. What are Helophilous?
Ans. Halophytes growing in marshy places
near seashore from a special vegetation
known as the mangrove or tidal woodland.
These are also called helophilous
halophytes.
Thermoregulation in Plants
Q76. How plants are adapted to survive
in heat stress? / What are heat-stock
proteins?
• High temperature denatures the enzymes
and damages the metabolism.

• Plants use evaporative cooling to cope
with high temperature. Hot and dry
weather, however, causes water deficiency
resulting in closing of stomata, thus plants
suffer in such conditions.
• Most plants have adapted to survive in
heat stress as the plants of temperate
regions face the stress of 40°C and higher
temperature.
• The cells of these plants synthesize large
quantities of special proteins called heat-
shock proteins.

[REPORT ANY MISTAKE AT: FREEILM786@GMAIL.COM]                                                 [WEBSITE: WWW.FREEILM.COM]

--- Page 16 ---
• These proteins embrace enzymes and
other proteins thus help to prevent their
denaturation.
Q77. Low temperature alters the fluidity
of the cell membrane, how come plants of
these regions are adapted?
Ans. Low temperature
• Low temperature alters the fluidity of the
cell membrane, because lipids of the
membrane become locked into crystalline
structures, which affects the transport of
the solutes. The structure of the membrane
proteins is also affected.
• Plants respond to cold stress by increasing
proportion of unsaturated fatty acids,
which help membrane to maintain structure
at low temperature by preventing crystal
formation. This adaptation requires time.
Because of this reason, rapid chilling of
plants is more stressful than gradual drop in
air temperature.
Q78. How does the plant native to cold
regions prevent ice-crystal formation in
freezing temperature?
Ans. Freezing temperature
Freezing temperature causes ice crystal
formation. The confinement of ice formation
around cell wall does not affect as badly and
plants survive.
• However, formation of ice crystals within
protoplasm perforates membranes and
organelles hence killing the cells.
Adaptations: The plants native to cold
region such as oaks, maples, roses and other
plants have adapted to bring changes in
solutes composition of the cells, which
causes cytosol to super cool without ice
formation, although ice crystals may form in
the cell walls.
Movements in Plants
Q79. Define tropic movements. Name the
major types of tropic movements in plants.
Ans. Tropic movements: The growth
movements in plants that are triggered by an
external stimulus, are collectively called
tropic movements or tropisms.
• Such movements occur as a curvature of
whole organ towards or away from stimuli
such as light, touch, chemical, water and
gravity.
• Following are the major types of tropic
movements in plants.
1. Phototropism
2. Geotropism
3. Thigmotropism
4. Chemotropism
5. Hydrotropism
Q80. Differentiate between phototropism and geotropism.
Phototropism
• It is the movement of parts of plant, in
response to stimulus of light and is
caused by the differential growth of part
of a plant like stem or root.
• The tips of shoots usually show positive
phototropism while roots show negative
phototropism.
Geotropism
• It is the movement of plant parts in
response to gravity.
• Roots display positive geotropism and
shoots negative geotropism.

| :--- | :--- |
| • It is the type of movement in plants in response to stimulus of touch, for example climbing vines. | • It is the type of movement in plants in response to some chemicals is called chemotropism. |
