Photoperiodism
Q82. Define photoperiodism.
Ans. The response to changes in day length that enables plants to adapt to seasonal changes in their environment is termed as photoperiodism. Simply, it is response of plants to the length of day and night e.g., in strawberries flowering is induced by dark periods longer than a critical length.
Q83. Classify plants on the basis of photoperiodism. / How did Garner and Allard classified plants on the basis of day length?
Ans. Effect of photoperiodism was first studied in 1920 by Garner and Allard. They studied that tobacco plant flowers only after exposure to a series of short days.
• Tobacco plant naturally flowers under same conditions, in autumn, but flowering could be induced by artificially exposing to short days.
• With further studies they were able to classify flowering plants into long-day plants, which require long days for flowering, short-day plants, which require short days for flowering and day-neutral plants which flower without being influenced by photoperiod.
Q84. What are phytochromes? describe its forms.
Ans. Phytochrome, a photoreceptor protein exists in two forms i.e., P660 and P730.
P660 is a quiescent form. It absorbs red light at a wavelength of 660 nm and is converted to active P730 which absorbs far red light at 730 nm and is converted to P660.
• In nature, the P660 to P730 conversion takes place in day light and P730 to P660 conversion occurs in the dark.
• The rate at which P730 is converted to P660 provides the plant with a “clock” for measuring the duration of darkness.
Q85. P730 to P660 interconversion act as plant time regulator for flowering Comment.
Ans. It has been found that red light inhibits flowering in short-day plants but promotes flowering in long-day plants, under conditions during which flowering normally takes place.
• This observation led to the hypothesis that the P730 to P660 interconversion might be the plant time-regulator for flowering.
• According to this hypothesis, P730, converted from P660 by the absorption of red light, would inhibit flowering in short day plants but promote flowering in long day plants.
• Because P730 accumulates in the day and diminishes at night, short day plants could flower only if the night were long enough, during which a great amount of P730 would not be completely inactivated, so that

--- Page 18 ---
enough P730 would remain at the end of
night to promote flowering.
Vernalization
Q86. Define vernalization. Write its
significance.
Ans. The process of induction of flowering
in plants by exposing them to a certain low
(chilling) temperature is called vernalisation.
• For some plants, vernalisation is an
absolute requirement while in some cases
it simply assists in inducing flowering.
• The duration of low temperature (chilling)
treatment varies from four days to three
months.
Significance
• Photoperiodism and vernalisation serve to
synchronise the reproductive behaviour of
plants with their environment, ensuring
reproduction at favourable times of year.
• They also ensure that members of the same
species flower at the same time,
encouraging cross pollination for genetic
variability.

INQUISITIVE QUESTIONS
Q1. Can you explain the hypothesis regarding the opening and closing of
stomata?
Ans. The guard cells function as multisensory hydraulic valves. The two hypotheses which
may explain the opening and closing of stomata are starch sugar hypothesis and influx of k+
ion.
Starch Sugar Hypothesis
In 1856, German botanist H. Van Mohl proposed that guard cells in leaf epidermis are solely
responsible for photosynthesis, producing sugars during the day. As sugar concentration
increases in guard cells, the water potential drops. Water moves into guard cells causing them
to become turgid and open the stomata and vice versa.
Influx of K+ ion
The opening of stomata in plants is facilitated by the active transport of potassium ions (K+)
into guard cells, which reduces their osmotic potential. This influx of K- leads to water
entering the guard cells through osmosis, causing them to become turgid and open the stomata.

--- Page 19 ---
[WANT TO GET ALL SUBJECT NOTES: WWW.FREEILM.COM]                                                               [WEBSITE: WWW.FREEILM.COM]

Q2. What mechanisms enable carnivorous plants to supplement their nutrient
uptake despite being autotrophs?
Ans. Insectivorous plants supplement organic molecules into their food in addition to
inorganic nutrients. These organic chemicals are acquired through the process of capturing
and breaking down insects and tiny animals. All insectivorous plants are true autotrophs.
However, their development accelerates when they capture prey. Apparently, nitrogenous
compounds of animal body are of benefit to these plants. The captured insects are broken
down by enzymes that are released by the leaves. Pitcher plant, venus fly trap and sundew are
some of the known insectivorous plants.
Pitcher plant: Pitcher plant has leaves modified into a sac or a pitcher, partly filled with
water.
Venus-fly trap: Venus-fly trap has a “trap” consisting of two lobes that are hinged at the end
of each leaf.
Sundew catches its prey with shiny drops of “dew”, where the plant’s common name comes
from.
Q3. How can you say that parenchyma and sclerenchyma provide support to
plants?
Ans. Support in Plants
Supporting tissues play an important role in maintaining the structural integrity, support and
flexibility of plants. These tissues consist of parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma, xylem
and phloem.
1. Parenchyma
The parenchyma cells of the epidermis, cortex, and pith absorb water. This water creates an
internal hydrostatic pressure known as turgor pressure that maintains the rigidity of cells.
2. Sclerenchyma
The cells of sclerenchyma tissue possess thick secondary cell walls. These walls are
saturated with lignin, an organic compound that confers strength and rigidity to the
walls.
Q4. How do the annual rings depict climatic variability?
Ans. Annual rings are formed due to the
seasonal activity of the cambium layer in trees.
This process is influenced by environmental
factors and results in the production of two
distinct types of wood each year: spring wood
(early wood) and autumn wood (late wood).
These rings provide valuable information about
the age of the tree and the environmental
conditions experienced during each growing
season.

[REPORT ANY MISTAKE AT: FREEILM786@GMAIL.COM]                                                               [WEBSITE: WWW.FREEILM.COM]

--- Page 20 ---
The cambium is a meristematic tissue that generates new vascular tissues i.e., xylem and
phloem.
In spring: In spring, when conditions are favourable, the cambium is highly active,
producing large volume of xylem with wider vessels, resulting in lighter-coloured spring
wood.
In autumn: As the season changes to autumn, the cambium's activity decreases. It produces
fewer xylem elements, which are narrower and denser, leading to the formation of darker
autumn wood.
Q5. How does pressure flow theory explain the movement of sugars through a
plant?
Ans. Pressure flow theory: The pressure-flow theory, also known as the mass-flow
hypothesis, is the most widely accepted explanation for the transport of sugars in plants
through the phloem. This process of translocation moves sugar from the source (where they
are synthesized) to the sink (where they are consumed or stored). This theory relies on the
principle of osmotic pressure differences between source and sink regions.
There is a higher water potential at the source end while a lower water potential at the sink
end. The difference in water potential causes water to flow from source to sink. Since sucrose
is dissolved in water, it is carried along from source to sink along with water.
Q6. What strategies would you adopt to induce flowering in a plant?
Ans. Flowering can be induced by growing plants in controlled environment.
1. By variation in critical length and dark periods
• For inducing flowering in short day plants, keep them in light for short duration and
increasing their dark period artificially.
• For inducing flowering in long day plants, keeping them in dark for shorter duration
can induce flowering.
2. By temperature treatment
Biennial and perennial plants are stimulated to flowering by exposure to low temperature
(chilling) from four days to three months, this process is also called vernalization.

Unit 9: Human Digestive System

Long Questions

DESCRIPTIVE QUESTIONS

ANATOMY AND PHYSIOLOGY OF DIGESTIVE SYSTEM

Q1. Define Digestion. Mention its importance and components of digestive
system.
Ans. Definition: Digestion is a process by which the body breaks down food into smaller
absorbable components.
Components
Human digestive system is composed of gastrointestinal (GI) tract and accessory digestive
organs. The GI tract is a continuous tube that extends from mouth to anus. Oral cavity is the
first part of GI tract. Accessory digestive organs of oral
cavity are the salivary glands.
Oral Cavity: It is a cavity immediately after the
opening of mouth.
Functions of oral cavity
(i) Selection of food: The muscular tongue plays role in
selection of food through its taste bonds. When food
enters the oral cavity, it is tasted and physically felt. If
the taste or smell is unpleasant or if hard objects like
bone or dirt are present in the food, it is rejected. The
senses of smell and sight also play role in the selection
of food.
(ii) Mechanical digestion of food: The ingested food is
physically broken down by the teeth through a process
called mastication (chewing). Chewing converts food
into smaller and more manageable pieces. This increases
their surface area for enzymatic action.
(iii) Chemical digestion of food: During the process of chewing salivary glands secrete
saliva into oral cavity. There are three pairs of salivary glands.
a. Sublingual glands: Situated below the tongue.
b. Submaxillary glands: Located behind the jaws.
★ Note: All questions and paragraphs marked with a star ★ are explanations of the Box
Information provided in the textbook.

[REPORT ANY MISTAKE AT: FREEILM786@GMAIL.COM] [WEBSITE: WWW.FREEILM.COM]

--- Page 2 ---
c. Parotid glands: Located in front of ears.
Composition of Saliva
Saliva is composed of:
(i) Water and Mucus: These moisten and lubricate the food.
(ii) Bicarbonate ions: These act as buffer to control pH of the oral cavity.
(iii) Thiocyanate ions: They kill microorganisms.
• pH of saliva: Fresh saliva is alkaline with pH 8 but it quickly loses CO2 and pH becomes 6.
• Salivary amylase: Saliva contains amylase which partially digests the polysaccharides
(starch and glycogen) to a disaccharide (maltose).
Bolus: After chemical and mechanical digestion in the oral cavity the food in the oral cavity
takes the form of a small moist mass called a bolus.
Q2. Explain the process of swallowing of food.
Ans. Pharynx is the cavity behind the month (oral cavity). It is the common passageway
for both the digestive and respiratory tracts. Bolus is pushed to the back of mouth and is
swallowed through the pharynx.
Swallowing of food
(i) During swallowing the tongue moves upwards and backwards against the roof of the
mouth this forces the bolus to the back of oral cavity.
(ii) Soft palate is raised against the back wall of pharynx, this closes the passage between
nasal cavity and pharynx.
(iii) At the same time larynx moves upwards and epiglottis (a flap of cartilage over glottis) is
lowered. This closes the opening of trachea (wind pipe).
(iv) In this way the bolus passes over the trachea and enters oesophagus.

The beginning of the swallowing action is voluntary but once the food reaches the back of

Q3. Explain movement of food through oesophagus.
Ans. 1. After being swallowed, the food enters the
tube oesophagus. It connects the pharynx to the
stomach. The digestive action of saliva continues in
oesophagus.
2. Oesophagus is 25cm long and its lower end opens
in stomach.
3. Food passes through oesophagus to stomach by a
process called peristalsis.
Motility of Alimentary Canal
Movement in the alimentary canal is of two types i.e.
peristalsis and segmentation.
1. Peristalsis: It is the rhythmic sequence of waves
of contraction in the smooth muscles of the walls of
alimentary canal. Peristalsis squeezes the food down
along the oesophagus and other parts of alimentary
canal.
Anti-peristalsis: Occasionally the peristaltic
movements may reverse in a process called
antiperistalsis. In this food is pushed from intestine
back into stomach and oral cavity. This is also called
as vomiting.
Hunger contractions: These are also peristaltic
movements caused by low glucose levels in blood,
creating the uncomfortable sensation known as hunger
pangs.
2. Segmentation: The small and large intestines also
have rings of smooth-muscles which contract and
relax repeatedly. These contractions and relaxations
create back and forth movement in the same place,
called segmentation. This movement mixes the food
with digestive secretions and thus increases the
efficiency of absorption.
Sphincters: The exit of food from the oesophagus to
the stomach is controlled by lower oesophageal
sphincter or cardiac sphincter (because it is near the
heart). This opens in response to the pressure exerted
by food. It also prevents back flow of stomach
contents into the oesophagus.
Q4. Explain structure and function of stomach.
Ans. Structure

--- Page 4 ---
1. Shape: It is an elastic muscular bag (J-shaped) situated after oesophagus and before
duodenum.
2. Location: It is located in the left side in abdominal cavity, below the diaphragm.
3. Portions
Stomach has three portions.
(i) Cardiac portion: It is present immediately after oesophagus.
(ii) Fundus portion: It is present on a side of cardiac portion.
(iii)Pyloric portion: It is located beneath the cardiac portion.
Stomach wall
1. Serosa: It is the outer covering and provides protection.
2. Muscularis Externa: There are three layers of smooth muscles outer longitudinal, middle
circular and inner oblique muscles.
3. Mucosa and Submucosa: Mucosa is the inner lining of the stomach. It contains gastric
glands that produce digestive juice. Submucosa lies beneath mucosa it contains blood
vessels, lymphatic vessel and nerve fibers.

Functions
1. Mechanical digestion: The muscular walls of stomach contract vigorously and help in
churning (shaking) and mixing of food with stomach secretions. The contractions also
generate enough heat to melt the solid fats.

--- Page 5 ---
2. Chemical digestion: The mucosa of stomach posses many tubular gastric glands which
open through the deep depressions called gastric pits. Each gastric gland has epithelial cells
and three secretary cells.
(i) Mucous cells: These secrete mucous which is thick secretion that covers the inside of
the stomach and protects it from HCl and digestive enzymes.
(ii) The parietal (oxyntic) cells: These secrete hydrochloric acid. It adjusts the pH of
stomach contents to about 2-3. HCl also softens the food and activates the protein digesting
enzyme, pepsinogen to pepsin. It also kills microorganisms.
(iii) Chief Cells: These cells secrete enzyme pepsinogen (inactive form of pepsin).
All the secretions of gastric glands are collectively called gastric juice. When the bolus
enters the stomach the gastric glands secrete gastric juice. H+ ions of HCl activate
pepsinogen into pepsin. Pepsin breaks protein into polypeptides (Contain 10-50 amino
acids) and peptides (Contain 2 to 50 amino acids).
Chyme: After about three to four hours after meal, stomach contents are mixed and in the
form of semi-liquid acidic mass called chyme. Pyloric sphincter controls the release of
chyme into small intestine.
★ Pyrosis or Heart Burn
Sometimes there is a back flush of acidic chyme from stomach into the oesophagus. It
causes a painful burning sensation in the chest and this is called Pyrosis or Heart burn.
Q5. Explain digestion in small intestine.
Ans. Small intestine is largest part of alimentary canal. It starts from stomach and ends at
large intestine. It has diameter of 2-3 cm and 6 metres' length. Food is not only digested but
also absorbed in small intestine.
Parts: Small intestine consists of three parts i.e. duodenum, jejunum and ileum.
1. Duodenum
(i) It is first 20-25 cm long part of small intestine. It is concerned with digestion of food. It
contains glands, which produce an alkaline secretion containing bicarbonate.
(ii) Two main secretions are poured into duodenum.
(a) Pancreatic juice: It is secreted from pancreas. It is slightly alkaline (pH 8) due to
presence of bicarbonate. It neutralizes the acidity of chyme. Important enzymes of
pancreatic juice are.
(i) Pancreatic amylase: It digests polysaccharides into maltose and even glucose.
(ii) Trypsinogen: It is an inactive form. Another enzyme enterokinase (secreted by walls of
duodenum) activates trypsinogen into trypsin, which digests proteins into polypeptides.
(iii)Chymotrypsin and carboxypeptidase, which digest proteins into smaller peptides and
then into amino acids.
(iv) Pancreatic lipase, which digest lipids into glycerol and fatty acids.
(v) Pancreatic nucleases, which digest DNA and RNA into nucleotides.
(b) Bile: It is the secretion of liver. Before its release it is stored in gallbladder. It contains
salts which emulsify fat and break them into small droplets (emulsion). These droplets
provide large surface areas for effective action of lipid digesting enzymes.
2. Jejunum and Ileum: Jejunum is 2.4 meters long, next to duodenum. Ileum is the last
three fifth i.e., about 3.5 metres long part of small intestine. These parts carry out the rest of

--- Page 6 ---
digestion and absorption of food. The walls of jejunum and ileum contain glands which
secrete intestinal juice. It contains various enzymes; e.g.,
• Aminopeptidase which digests polypeptides into dipeptides.
• Erypsin digests dipeptides into amino acids.
• Lipase digests fats into fatty acids and glycerol.
• Maltase digests maltose into glucose
• Sucrase digests sucrose into glucose and fructose
• Lactase digests lactose into glucose and galactose.
Chyle: In jejunum chyme after digestion is converted into alkaline emulsion called chyle.
Q6. Explain absorption of digested food and water.
Ans. The absorption of digested food, water, and dissolved minerals occurs in jejunum
and ileum. Inner wall of jejunum and ileum contains large circular folds. These folds have
several finger like projections called villi.
Structure of Villus
Each villus is richly supplied with blood capillaries and a vessel of lymphatic system, called
lacteal. The blood capillaries and lacteal are covered by a single-cell thick epithelium.
The epithelial cells of villi have many cytoplasmic projections, called microvilli. The total
surface area of absorption becomes extraordinarily increased due to villi and microvilli.
★ Appearance: Due to presence of folds and numerous villi the internal surface of jejunum
and ileum appears velvety.

Figure: Intestinal wall and detailed structure of villi
Absorption of simple sugars and amino acids
• Simple sugars (e.g., glucose) and amino acids are absorbed by diffusion or active
transport into the epithelial cells of villi.

--- Page 7 ---
• From here, these molecules enter the blood capillaries of villi.
• Blood capillaries of villi join to form hepatic portal vein which carries sugars and amino acids to liver.
• Liver stores extra glucose and amino acids in the form glycogen and proteins respectively.
• From liver, the required amounts of these products pass to heart via hepatic vein.
Absorption of Fatty acids and glycerol
• The products of fat digestion i.e., fatty acids and glycerol are absorbed by passive transport into the epithelial cells of villi. Here they combine to form triglycerides.
• The triglycerides are coated with proteins and small droplets, called chylomicrons.
• The chylomicrons enter the lacteals of villi.
• From the lacteals, the chylomicrons move into thoracic lymphatic duct, and then into the blood stream. Chylomicrons in blood are hydrolysed by the enzymes of blood plasma back into fats and proteins.
• Fats are further hydrolyzed into fatty acids and glycerol and enter the body cells.
★ Absorption of fats
Fats are insoluble in water. So, they cannot be attacked readily by lipase enzymes of pancreatic juice. Bile salts act as detergent molecules. They break fats into droplets and keep them separate from one another.
Q7. Describe structure and function of large intestine.
Ans. Structure of Large Intestine
1. It is much shorter than small intestine and makes the last meter of the intestinal tract.
2. It is involved in the absorption of water and salts and vitamin K from the lumen (cavity) of intestine into the blood. The large intestine is not convoluted (coiled) and its inner surface does not possess villi.
Parts: Large intestine has three parts.
a. Caecum
It is a blind sac that projects from the area of large intestine between ileum and colon. From the blind end of caecum, vermiform (finger like) process arises called as appendix. In humans appendix has no function so it is vestigial (non-functional).
b. Colon
Next to caecum is the colon. It has an ascending, a transverse and a descending limb. Its main function is to absorb water. As the water is absorbed, the remaining material becomes more solid. These wastes products are called faeces, these consist of large number of bacteria, undigested plant fibres (e.g., cellulose), and other food stuff, sloughed off mucosal cells, bile pigments and water.
c. Rectum
It is the last part of large intestine where faeces are stored for short time. At its distal end, the rectum opens out through anus. Anus is surrounded by two sphincters; the internal sphincter is made of smooth muscles and the outer is made of striated muscles. When the rectum is filled up with faeces, it gives rise to a defecation reflex. The defecation reflex can be consciously inhibited in adults but in infants it is controlled involuntarily. Later on the child learns to control this reflex voluntarily.

--- Page 8 ---
Vitamin K Production: Many bacteria, e.g E.coli, live and actively divide in the colon.
They produce amino acids and vitamin K. Vitamin K is necessary for blood coagulation. It
is absorbed from the large intestine into the blood.
Q8. Write note on control of Egestion.
Ans. Egestion is removal of the undigested food from the rectum. It is an involuntary act
in infants while voluntary in the adults. There are two stages of egestion control i.e.
Neurological and muscular development.
1. In infants, egestion is an involuntary reflex mediated by the spinal cord. Here the rectal
distension triggers automatic relaxation of the internal anal sphincter and expulsion of waste.
This occurs because the higher centres (cerebral cortex) are not yet fully developed.
2. In adults, because cerebral cortex is mature, this allows conscious regulation of external
anal sphincter to delay or initiate defecation.
This transition (change) reflects the integration (combination) of reflex pathways with
cognitive (concious) control, adapting to social and environmental demands.
This means that in adults when brain is fully developed, motor neurons from cerebral cortex,
change this involuntary action of egestion, controlled by neurons of spinal cord only in
infants, to the voluntary action in adults. So adults can control (initiate or inhibit) egestion
voluntarily as per situation or requirement.
Q9. Write note an accessory dige tive organs.
Ans. 1. Liver and Gallbladder
i. Liver plays a vital role in digestion by producing bile, which is essential for fat digestion.
Bile emulsifies fats (during emulsification large fat globules are converted into smaller
ones). This makes them easier for enzymes to digest.
ii. Liver also modifies nutrients absorbed from the small intestine.
iii. It detoxifies the harmful substances.
iv. It synthesizes proteins.
v. It stores glycogen for energy.
vi. Gall bladder stores and concentrate bile produced by liver. When food enters the small
intestine, bile is released from the gall bladder into duodenum through bile duct.
2. Pancreas
i. It is a large gland situated just ventral to the stomach.
ii. It has exocrine and endocrine portion. The exocrine (with duct) portion secretes
pancreatic juice through pancreatic duct, which joins into the common bile duct from the
liver and enters the duodenum.
iii. Pancreatic juice contains enzymes for the digestion of all groups of food. The main
enzymes are trypsin, chymotrypsin, lipases, amylases, nucleases etc.
iv. The endocrine (ductless) portion of pancreas secretes insulin and glucagon hormones into
extracellular fluid from where they diffuse into nearby capillaries.
Q10. Write short note on hormonal control of the secretions of pancreas and
liver.
Ans. 1. The release of secretions from pancreas and liver is controlled by hormones.
2. When chyme enters duodenum from stomach, its acidity stimulates duodenal walls to
release secretin.

--- Page 9 ---
3. Similarly, the partially digested proteins and fats present in chyme stimulate the duodenal
walls to secrete another hormone, cholecystokinin (CCK). Both these hormones stimulate
pancreas to release pancreatic juice, and gallbladder to release bile.
Cholecystokinin
Cholecystokinin is a hormone produced in the small intestine that play a key role in
digestion by triggering the gall bladder to release bile into small intestine, stimulating
pancreatic enzyme release and regulating appetite.

Figure: Accessory Digestive Organs

Q11. Explain storage and metabolic role of liver.
Ans. The liver performs many important functions like storing nutrient and regulating
metabolism.
1. Storage
• It stores excess nutrients from the food and releases them when body needs energy or
building materials.
• The stored nutrients include glucose (stored as glycogen), vitamins (like A, D, B12, and
K), minerals (e.g., iron and copper) and fats along with fat-soluble substances.
2. Metabolic role
a. Conversion: It converts excess glucose into glycogen and back when needed.
b. Breakdown: It breaks down fats to produce energy.
3. Synthesis
(i) If forms cholesterol and lipoproteins.
(ii) It synthesizes urea by removing ammonia produced from amino acids. Urea is then
excreted in urine.
4. Detoxification: It breaks down and removes toxins, drugs, and alcohol from the blood.
5. Hormonal Regulation: Liver also helps in breaking down and regulating hormones.
Q12. Describe the hormonal and nervous regulation of gastric acid secretion.
Ans. The secretion of gastric juice is regulated by both the nervous system and hormonal

--- Page 10 ---
mechanisms.
1. In reaction to the smell, sight or thought of food, the medulla of brain sends message to
the gastric glands to secrete small amounts of gastric juice.
2. When food arrives in stomach, the distension (expansion) of stomach and decrease in pH
of gastric contents stimulate more secretion and powerful contraction.
3. The presence of proteins in food stimulate special endocrine cells present in the mucosa
of stomach to release a hormone called gastrin. Gastrin is carried by blood to gastric
glands where it stimulates them to produce and secrete more gastric juice.
4. When food moves from stomach to small intestine, a hormone called somatostatin stops
the release of hydrochloric acid.

Unit 9: Human Digestive System

Short Questions

SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS EXERCISE

Q1. What is the main function of the
digestive system?
Ans. Function of digestive system is to
break down food into smaller and
absorbable components.

Q2. What is the mode of action of
saliva in mouth?
Ans. Saliva has following actions.
1. It moistens and lubricates food.
2. Bicarbonate ions kill microorganisms.
3. Salivary amylase partly digests the
polysaccharides (starch and glycogen) to
disaccharide (maltose).

Q3. What is role of tongue in the
mouth?
Ans. During swallowing the tongue moves
upwards and backwards against the roof of
the mouth. With this bolus is pushed to the
back of the mouth and is swallowed through
the pharynx.

Q4. What role does the epiglottis play
during swallowing?
Ans. During swallowing the epiglottis
closes the opening of trachea. In this way
bolus passes over the trachea and enters
oesophagus.

[REPORT ANY MISTAKE AT: FREEILM786@GMAIL.COM] [WEBSITE: WWW.FREEILM.COM]

--- Page 2 ---
Q5. What is the composition of gastric
juice?
Ans. Gastric juice contains
1. Mucous secreted by mucous cells.
2. Hydrochloric acid by parietal (oxyntic)
cells.
3. Enzyme pepsinogen by chief cells.
Q6. Why is hydrochloric acid (HCl)
important in the stomach?
Ans. Hydrochloric acid is important in
following ways.
1. It adjusts the pH of stomach content to
about 2-3.
2. It softens the food.
3. It activates the pepsinogen.
4. It kills the microorganisms.
Q7. What is the difference between
bolus and chyme?
Ans. 1. Bolus: After mechanical and
chemical digestive processes in the oral
cavity food mass is in the form of a small
moist mass called bolus.
2. Chyme: About three to four hours after a
meal the stomach contents have been
sufficiently mixed into a semi-liquid mass
called chyme.
Q8. Which organ produces bile, and
what is its function?
Ans. Bile is secreted by liver. It contains
salts which emulsify fats and break them
into small droplets (emulsion) this provides
large surface area for effective action of
lipids digesting enzymes.
Q9. Differentiate between physical and
chemical digestion.
Ans. Physical (mechanical) digestion: In
this ingested food in physically broken down
by the teeth through a process called
mastication. This converts food into smaller
pieces thus increasing the surface area for
enzymatic action.
Chemical digestion: It is process of
breaking down large insoluble food
molecules into smaller, soluble molecules
using enzymes e.g. conversion of starch into
maltose by enzyme amylase.
Q10. What do you understand by
emulsification of fats?
Ans. During emulsification, fats are
broken down into small droplets. These
droplets provide large surface areas for
effective action of lipid digesting enzymes.
Q11. What is of the role of the pyloric
sphincter in digestion?
Ans. Pyloric sphincter is a muscular valve
at the bottom of stomach. It regulates the
release of chyme from the stomach to the
small intestine.
Q12. How do villi and microvilli help in
nutrient absorption?
Ans. Each villus is richly supplied with
blood capillaries and lymphatic vessels.
These are covered by single cell thick
epithelium. The epithelial cells of villi have
countless cytoplasmic projection called
microvilli. The total surface area of
absorption becomes extraordinarily large
due to villi and microvilli.
Q13. What are the main functions of the
large intestine?
Ans. Following are the main functions of
large intestine.
i. It is involved in the absorption of water,
salts and vitamin K.
ii. Many bacteria live and divide in this
large intestine (colon). They produce
amino acids and vitamin K, necessary
for coagulation of blood.
Q14. What causes jaundice in the
digestive system?
Ans. When bile pigments are prevented
from leaving the digestive tract, they may
accumulate in blood causing a condition
known as jaundice.

--- Page 3 ---
Q15. How does stress negatively impact
digestion?
Ans. Stress impacts digestion by
(i) Decreased production of digestive
enzymes.
(ii) Slowing down the process, i.e. slow gut
motility.
(iii) Increasing stomach acid due to release of
stress hormones like cortisol.
(iv) Cause entering of bacteria into blood
stream.
(v) Increased gas production or diarrhoea.

SLO BASED SHORT QUESTION ANSWERS
Anatomy and Physiology of Digestive
System
Q16. Give parts of digestive system of
man.
Ans. Following are the parts of digestive
system of man.
a) Gastrointestinal tract (GI)
b) Accessory digestive organs i.e. liver and
pancreas, gall bladder and salivary
glands.
Q17. Define GI tract and accessory
digestive organs.
Ans. The GI tract is a continuous tube that
extends from mouth to anus. It includes oral
cavity, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, small
intestine and large intestine. The accessory
digestive organs include the salivary glands,
liver, gallbladder and pancreas.
Q18. Define mastication. Write its role
in digestion.
Ans. It is also known as chewing. In this
process the food is broken down into smaller
and more manageable pieces by using teeth.
Mastication increase the surface area of food
for enzymatic action.
Q19. Name three pairs of salivary
glands. Give composition of saliva.
Ans.
i. Sublingual glands
ii. Sub maxillary glands
iii. Parotid gland
Composition of saliva: Saliva is composed
of following components.
• Water and mucous
• Bicarbonate and thiocyanate ions
• Salivary amylase (enzyme)
Q20. Digestion is crucial for converting
food into energy. Comment.
Ans. Digestion is crucial for converting
food into energy and raw materials required
for growth, repair and maintenance of body
functions. It supports the immune system,
provides essential nutrients and ensures
overall health. Efficient digestion prevents
nutrient deficiencies, supports metabolism
and maintains energy levels, making it vital
for sustaining life.
Q21. What is bolus? In which part of
respiratory system it is produced?
Ans. Bolus is a soft and moist mass od
chewed food, which is produced after
mastication due to physical and chemical
digestion of food in oral cavity.
★Q22. Is swallowing action voluntary or
involuntary action.
Ans. The beginning of the swallowing
action is voluntary but once the bolus
reaches the back of the mouth, swallowing
becomes involuntary.
Q23. What is function of epiglottis.
Ans. During swallowing epiglottis closes
the opening of trachea. In this way bolus
passes over the trachea and enters the
oesophagus.
Q24. What are lips? Give their
functions.
Ans. 1. Lips: Lips are made of highly
vascularized (with blood vessels) skeletal

--- Page 4 ---
muscle tissues and many sensory nerve
endings.
2. Functions of Lips
i. Lips help to retain food as is being
chewed.
ii. They also play a role in phonation of
sound (it means to central airflow and
shaping the vocal tract to produce
sounds).
Q25. Define peristalsis.
Ans. It is rhythmic sequence of waves of
contraction in the smooth muscles of the
walls of alimentary canal. Peristalsis
squeeze the food down along oesophagus
and other parts of alimentary canal.
Q26. What is meant by segmentation?

Ans. The contraction and relaxation of the
rings of smooth muscles in small and large
intestine is called segmentation. This creates
back and forth movement in the same place.
This movement mixes the food with
digestive secretions and improves
absorption.
Q27. What is antiperistalsis?
Ans. The reverse movements of peristalsis
are called antiperistalsis. In this food is
pushed from intestine back into the stomach
and oral cavity, leading to vomiting.
Q28. What is hunger pang?
Ans. It is an uncomfortable sensation
created by peristaltic movements triggered
by low blood glucose levels.
★Q29.What is pyrosis or heartburn?

Ans. Sometimes there is a back flush of
acidic chyme from stomach into the
oesophagus. It causes a painful burning
sensation in the chest. This is called heart
burn.
Q30. Name three portions of stomach.
Ans. 1. Cardiac portion
2. Fundus portion
3. Pyloric portion

Q31. Give composition of middle layer
of stomach.
Ans. The middle layer of stomach is made
of smooth muscles. There are three layers of
these muscles.
1. Outer longitudinal muscles.
2. Middle circular muscles.
3. Inner oblique muscles.
Q32. Give composition of gastric glands.

Ans. Each gastric gland contains epithelial
cells and three secretory cell.
1. Mucous cells – which secrete mucous.
2. Parietal cells – which secrete
hydrochloric acid.
3. Chief cells – which secrete enzyme
pepsinogen.
Q33. What do you know about Rennin?

Ans. In infants, the gastric juice contains
large amounts of rennin enzyme. This
enzyme coagulates milk proteins and delays
the passage of milk into small intestine. This
helps other enzymes to digest milk proteins.
Q34. What is chyme and pyloric
sphincter?
Ans. Chyme is a semi-liquid acidic mass
formed after three to four hours after a meal.
Pyloric sphincter is located between
pyloric end of stomach and duodenum. It
controls the release of chyme into the small
intestine.
★Q35.How mucosa of stomach is
protected?
Ans. The mucosa of stomach can get
damaged by hydrochloric acid and pepsin.
So mucosa is protected in two ways.
1. By coating of viscous mucous.
2. Bicarbonate ions which neutralize acid.
Q36. Name the hormones secreted by
stomach. Also write its function.
Ans. Gastrin is the hormone secreted by
stomach. It is carried by blood to gastric

--- Page 5 ---
[WANT TO GET ALL SUBJECT NOTES: WWW.FREEILM.COM]                                [WEBSITE: WWW.FREEILM.COM]

glands where it stimulates them to produce
and secrete more gastric juice.
Q37. What is pancreatic juice? Write
the names of enzymes present in it.
Ans. It is the secretion of pancreas and is
poured into duodenum. It is slightly alkaline
(pH 8) due to presence of bicarbonate. It
neutralizes the acidity of chyme. The
important enzymes in pancreatic juice are:
(i) Pancreatic amylase which digests
polysaccharides into maltose and even
glucose.
(ii) Trypsinogen which is in inactive form.
Another enzyme enterokinase (secreted by
the walls of duodenum) activates
trypsinogen into trypsin which digests
proteins into polypeptides.
(iii) Chymotrypsin and carboxypeptidase,
which digest proteins into smaller peptides
and then into amino acids.
(iv) Pancreatic lipase which digests lipids
to glycerol and fatty acids.
(v) Pancreatic nucleases which digest DNA
and RNA into nucleotides.
★Q38. What is jaundice?
Ans. If bile pigments, are prevented from
leaving digestive tract, they may accumulate
in blood, causing a condition known as
jaundice.
Q39. Write function of enterokinase.

Ans. It converts inactive trypsinogen into
active trypsin, which digest proteins into
smaller peptides and then into amino acids.
Q40. Give composition and action of
bile.
Ans. Bile contains salts, water and
bilirubin pigment. Its function is
emulsification of fats.
Q41. Differentiate between chyme and
chyle.
Ans. Chyme is a semi-liquid acidic mass
formed in stomach after three to four hours
of meal. While chyle is the chyme converted

into alkaline emulsion by the action of
intestinal juice.
Q42. Differentiate between villi and
microvilli and give their significance.

Ans. Villi are the finger like projections
present on the folds on inner side of wall of
jejunum and ileum. Epithelial cells of villi
have many cytoplasmic projections called
microvilli.
Q43. What is lacteal? Give its function.

Ans. It is a small lymphatic vessel found in
the villi of small intestine. It absorbs fats
and fat-soluble vitamins.
★Q44. What is significance of villi and
microvilli?
Ans. They increase the total surface area
of absorption. Due to presence of folds and
numerous villi, the internal surface of
jejunum and ileum appears velvety.
Q45. What are chylomicrons?
Ans. The products of fat digestion i.e.
fatty acids and glycerol are absorbed into
epithelial cells of villi. Here they combine to
form triglycerides. The triglycerides are
coated with proteins to form small droplets
called chylomicrons.
Q46. What is appendix?
Ans. Caecum is a blind sac that projects
from the area of large intestine between
ileum and colon. From the blind end of
caecum there arises a finger-like process
called vermiform appendix. In human
digestive system appendix performs no
function so it is vestigial (non-functional).
★Q47. What is appendicitis and
appendectomy?
Ans. Appendicitis is the inflammation of
the appendix. It is usually due to bacterial
infection. The infected appendix must be
removed surgically otherwise it may burst
and inflammation may spread in entire
living of abdomen. The surgical removal of
appendix is called appendectomy.

[REPORT ANY MISTAKE AT: FREEILM786@GMAIL.COM]                                [WEBSITE: WWW.FREEILM.COM]

--- Page 6 ---
Q48. What is composition of Faeces?
Ans. Faeces contains large number of bacteria, indigestible plant fibers, undigested food stuff, sloughed off mucosal cells, bile pigments and water.
Q49. Name parts of large intestine and their function.
Ans.
1. Caecum: It helps in absorption of water and electrolytes.
2. Colon: It absorbs water and maintain electrolyte balance and formation of faeces.
3. Rectum: It stores faeces temporarily.
Q50. Name the portions of pancreas. Also write their secretions.
Ans. It has exocrine and endocrine portions. The exocrine (ducted) portion secretes its secretion i.e., pancreatic juice into pancreatic duct. Pancreatic juice contains enzymes for the digestion of all groups of food. Its major enzymes include trypsin, chymotrypsin, lipases, amylases, nucleases etc. The endocrine (ductless) portion of pancreas secretes its secretion i.e., insulin and glucagon hormones into extracellular fluid from where they diffuse into nearby capillaries.
★Q51. How gall stones are formed?
Ans. Cholesterol secreted by the liver, may precipitate in the gall bladder to produce gall stones which may block release of bile.
Q52. Give functions of secretin and cholecystokinin.
Ans. Both these hormones stimulate pancreas to release pancreatic juice and gall bladder to release bile.
Q53. Describe the role of liver in the storage of nutrients.
Ans. The liver performs many important functions, especially in storing nutrients and regulating metabolism. It stores excess nutrients from the food and releases them when the body needs energy or building materials. These nutrients stored in the liver include glucose (stored as glycogen), vitamins (like A, D, B12, and K), minerals (e.g., iron and copper) and fats and fat-soluble substances.
Q54. Liver play role in metabolism. Justify.
Ans. It helps in breaking down, building up, and converting substances in the body. For example, it converts excess glucose into glycogen and back when needed. It also breaks down fats to produce energy and forms cholesterol and lipoproteins. It converts amino acids and removes harmful ammonia by turning it into urea, which is excreted in urine. It breaks down and removes toxins, drugs and alcohol from the blood. The liver also helps in breaking down and regulating hormones.

INQUISITIVE QUESTIONS
Q.1 Why does the small intestine need both peristalsis and segmentation?
Ans. Because peristalsis squeezes the food down the gastrointestinal tract. While in
segmentation contractions and relaxation of rings of smooth muscles mixes the food with
digestive secretion and increase the efficiency of absorption as well.
Q.2 How does the liver help digestion without using enzymes?
Ans. Liver helps in digestion by production of bile. Bile contains salts which emulsify fats
and break than into small droplets. These droplets provide large surface areas for effective
action of lipids digesting enzymes.
Q.3 Why do we need bile if we already have enzymes for fat digestion?
Ans. Fats are insoluble in water. So they cannot be attacked readily by lipase (fat digesting
enzymes) of pancreatic juice. Also the bile salts act as detergent molecules they break fats
into droplet and keep them separate from one another.
Q.4 How does the pancreas “know” when to release its enzymes?
Ans. Secretin and cholecystokinin (CCK) hormones released by duodenal stimulate
pancreas to release pancreatic juice and gallbladder to release bile.
Q.5 Why are pancreatic secretions alkaline, not acidic?
Ans. Pancreatic secretions are alkaline, not acidic because;
1. To neutralize the acidic chyme from the stomach.
2. Creating an optional environment for pancreatic enzymes to function effectively.
